en: The Samādhi Enquired of by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, Scroll One;
also titled *The Concentrated Intent of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi Nation during the Western Jin Dynasty.
1. Chapter on the Great Awe-Inspiring Experience, First. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling within the borders of Magadha at the Dharma-Quiescence Hermitage.

Upon first attaining Buddhahood, his radiance shone with brilliant splendor; he proclaimed the treasury of the True Dharma, expounded the wisdom of the Tathāgata, elucidated the essentials of the three periods of time, and disseminated the concentration of the unimpeded jewel of the Path.

At that time, the Buddha, by means of this universal wisdom and infinite clarity, entered a state of perfect meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This concentration was tranquil and serene; suddenly, it was without form or image, nor did it have interior or exterior. It was still, beyond seeing or hearing. The meditative absorption in which he dwelt was vast and expansive, boundless and immeasurable—difficult to encounter and difficult to hear, met only once in billions of lifetimes. At this moment, he attained this concentration.
The Buddha’s meditative concentration is immeasurable; there is nothing it does not penetrate clearly. Through universal wisdom, he attains the power of all-encompassing knowledge.
Boundlessly pure, he extols the Tathāgata; being without a nest or cave, he manifests the Buddha-body through his transformative presence.

Having attained the profound and subtle phrase of great emptiness and stillness, he then propagated the infinite manifestations of the Buddhas; dwelling nowhere, he turned toward the practice of wisdom, his fame pervading the world and his light extolling the Tathāgata.
Arising at the opportune moment, he manifests a Buddha-land; through its single characteristic, he thoroughly realizes the signless, wherein the signless and the non-active are likewise signless.
His majestic radiance extends throughout the ten directions; such is the brilliance of the unsurpassed Buddha-concentration!
Throughout all lands to their furthest reaches, transformations were manifested simultaneously; throughout the entire world, there was none who was not struck with sublime wonder.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Samantabhadra, who, receiving the holy intent of the Buddha, thought to himself:
"The manifestations and transformations displayed today by the Tathāgata are such as have never been heard of or seen since time immemorial."
"Such a miraculous response must surely contain an extraordinary and inexhaustible essence; you should cause all the great Bodhisattvas of other regions to collectively receive and uphold it.
He then entered meditative absorption accordingly, emitting a great golden light that illuminated the lands of the ten directions.
Within that radiance, they scattered celestial flowers and incense and played celestial music; the music was gentle and harmonious, sounding as a single grand resonance.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva addressed the sons of noble family:
"Śākyamuni Buddha!"
"O sons of noble family! Today I shall expound a dharma never before heard;
whatever you desire shall be accomplished.
At that very moment, O Bodhisattva Mahāsattva!
As numerous as motes of dust, they all assembled there.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his great and sublime meditative absorption (*samādhi*), pervaded them all!

Beholding the entire multitude, there was nothing he did not clearly perceive: those who were born and those who had passed away, as well as their attainment and cessation; by means of his sublime absorption, there was nothing he did not fully comprehend.

The vast concentration reached everywhere, penetrating all without exception; he observed that those assembled were entirely bodhisattvas, all of them great *kumārabhūtas* and *mahāsattvas*, as numerous as the atoms of dust throughout the lands of the ten directions.
His resolve is entirely sublime and transcendent, peerless and extraordinary; he dwells in the highest offices, consecrated as supreme.
His Dharma-body is immeasurable and fully perfected; his fame and illustrious reputation spread universally throughout the ten directions.
Each abides in essential practice; their dwelling is like that of a Buddha. Their power is unrivaled, and they are as fierce as lions.
They have attained a diamond-like resolve, and their wisdom is unimpeded. Their merit and virtue are pure and profound, surpassing Mount Sumeru in weight.
The mind is likened to space, immeasurable; grasping the wisdom of *dhāraṇī*, one finds self-delight.
Having clearly understood the realm wherein all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, one fully attains the majestic adornments of the marks and signs of all Buddhas.
They are all able to manifest emanations throughout the ten directions, appearing in every world just as a Buddha moves others with his presence.
Their stride is peerless and their majestic spiritual power is uniquely supreme; they are able to let out the great lion’s roar throughout the ten directions.
With a diamond-like resolve, he crushes the enmity of Māra; he subdues them with compassion and brings them to submission through virtue alone.
He repels all non-Buddhists, moving forward and withdrawing with sovereign freedom; through his moral integrity and right contemplation, he provides succor and salvation to all.
They all sound the Dharma drum, have raised the Dharma banner, ring the Dharma gong, and erect the Dharma standard; wherever they travel or dwell, there is none who does not believe and understand.
At that time, the bodhisattvas assembled there each stood according to their respective names.
Their names were:
Bodhisattva Resolute Intention, Bodhisattva Transcending Intention, Bodhisattva Expounding Intention, and Bodhisattva Supreme Intention.
Bodhisattva Dānamati, Bodhisattva Nāgamati, Bodhisattva Phalamati, Bodhisattva Vinayamati, Bodhisattva Balamati,
Bodhisattva Viśālamati, Bodhisattva Anantamati, Bodhisattva Vimuktimati, Bodhisattva Paramamati,
Bodhisattva Devamati, Bodhisattva Yajñamati, and Bodhisattva Padamati.
...the Bodhisattva Kāryamati, the Bodhisattva Gauravamati, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati,
the Bodhisattva Śāntamati, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati, the Bodhisattva Ekacittamati, the Bodhisattva Ekalakṣaṇamati,
the Bodhisattva Sumati, the Bodhisattva Māyāmati, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Vegamati, and the Bodhisattva Manuṣyamati.
Buddhamati Bodhisattva, Arthavidbodhi Bodhisattva, Dīrghamati Bodhisattva, Acintya Bodhisattva, Anantamati Bodhisattva,
Vyūhamati Bodhisattva, Anantānta Bodhisattva, Vyūhamūla Bodhisattva, Gambhīradhātu Bodhisattva,
Samantaprasāda Bodhisattva, Nāgaprabha Bodhisattva, and Tejodhara Bodhisattva.
...Buddhakṣetra Bodhisattva, Cittarāja Bodhisattva, Ekavyūha Bodhisattva, Abhyudgata Bodhisattva, Prāptajñāna Bodhisattva,
Puṇyakriyā Bodhisattva, Dharmadīpta Bodhisattva, Lokaprabhāsa Bodhisattva, Lokadhara Bodhisattva,
Abhyudgataśānti Bodhisattva, Anuttara Bodhisattva, and Anuttama Bodhisattva.
the Bodhisattva Asama, the Bodhisattva Asamasama, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa, the Bodhisattva Prabhākara,
the Bodhisattva Śubhaprabha, the Bodhisattva Ekarāja, the Bodhisattva Vegakarma, the Bodhisattva Dharmavarṣa, the Bodhisattva Citradhara,
the Bodhisattva Samantavyūha, the Bodhisattva Prajñācakṣus, and the Bodhisattva Dharmottara.
...the Bodhisattva Wisdom Cloud, the Bodhisattva Earth-Bearer, the Bodhisattva Dharma King, the Bodhisattva Skillful Establishment,
the Bodhisattva Supreme Vow, the Bodhisattva Wondrous Conduct, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Treasury, the Bodhisattva Mind-King,
the Bodhisattva Cultivated Inner Mind, the Bodhisattva Universal Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Sustainer of the Power of the Transcended Stages, and the Bodhisattva Earth...
Bodhisattva Power-Force, Bodhisattva Good Moon, Bodhisattva Great Mountain Peak Chief, Bodhisattva Jewel Mountain Peak,
Bodhisattva Radiating Light, Bodhisattva Supreme Arena King, Bodhisattva Unassailable Arena, Bodhisattva Invincible Majesty,
Bodhisattva Great Dragon Chief, Bodhisattva Path Chief, and Bodhisattva Universal Tamer.
Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva Without Regress, Bodhisattva Holding the Buddha’s Auspicious Wheel, Bodhisattva Without Delusion, Bodhisattva Majestic Conduct,
Bodhisattva Without Conceptual Thought, Bodhisattva Immeasurable Intention, Bodhisattva Buddha-Transformation,
Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Treasury, Bodhisattva Wisdom Chief, Bodhisattva Dharma Radiance, and Bodhisattva Wisdom...
The Bodhisattva Saṃbhavagupta, the Bodhisattva Vṛṣṭabodhi, the Bodhisattva Antaprakāśa, the Bodhisattva Amūḍhaprakāśa, the Bodhisattva Vajrasamudgata,
the Bodhisattva Prajñāvīra, the Bodhisattva Vajraprabha, the Bodhisattva Prajñāvīramati, the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus,
the Bodhisattva Viśālacakṣus, the Bodhisattva Śubhamukha, and the Bodhisattva Tathāgata-sadṛśa.
The Bodhisattva Vīra, the Bodhisattva Dhṛtabuddhavajra, the Bodhisattva Vyūhasarvajñatā, the Bodhisattva Prajñālaṃkāra,
and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadraprajñāgarbha— bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as these,

as numerous as the atoms in the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions, equal to the void itself— all of whom had previously practiced together with the Bodhisattva Druma (in the Dan-ben manuscript: Suluya), cultivating the virtues of a bodhisattva until those virtues were fully perfected.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, suddenly rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I wish to question the Tathāgata regarding equal and perfect enlightenment; if you would grant me permission, I dare to speak my thoughts.”
The Buddha told Samantadarśin:
"Ask whatever you wish of the Tathāgata.
Following your own intent, I shall explain it for you so that you may be filled with joy."
At that time, Samantavaktra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One?
By means of how many inconceivable samādhis does a bodhisattva attain the practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, thereby reaching equality with the world-renouncing vows of Samantavīrya?"

Regarding the practice of the meditative discipline of adornment that he has cultivated, how does he exercise mastery over concentration to find delight therein, and by means of that power of concentration, how does he move all other concentrations?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain their ultimate source.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Samantadarśin, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
Samantadarśin Bodhisattva!"
I have thus extensively prepared the bodhimanda for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, proclaiming the essential doctrines to address these questions!
Such is the case, O Viśeṣacintin!
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra is now present in this assembly; he has attained inconceivable bodhisattva inspiration, cultivating the immeasurable practices of a bodhisattva;
he has attained inconceivable bodhisattva transformations, having purified the aspiration that is difficult for a bodhisattva to encounter.

They bring forth the non-regressive conduct of a bodhisattva’s birth; they cultivate immeasurable and vast pure practices; they transcend the immeasurable with equal ease; their eloquence is unimpeded.
They are never weary of great compassion toward all beings;
through their vows, they remain undisturbed until the very limits of existence.
"We should all together request him; he shall speak of the practices of the various meditative concentrations, right attainments, and sublime transformations.

At that time, the assembly, hearing the name of the noble being who had entered [samādhi], paid him all respect and looked toward him everywhere, desiring to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; yet they did not behold him, nor hear his voice, nor perceive his place of sitting.
Why is this? It is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata and the strength of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Samadarśin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Where is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva currently dwelling?
The Buddha told him,
“Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is in this very assembly, dwelling motionless to my left and right.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin and the great assembly, using their supernatural powers, searched for him everywhere but could not find his whereabouts; they addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"We do not see the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra nor his seat."
The World-Honored One said:
"It is so, son of good family!
You do not see the body of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra nor his seat."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra dwells in profound practice, he is ungraspable; because he abides in the conduct of wisdom without obstruction, he has attained the fierce power of a lion; because he has attained the unsurpassed miraculous transformations of a Buddha, he dwells in the limit of quiescent non-obstruction; because he abides in the treasury of the head of the Dharma-realm of the ten powers of a Buddha, he has realized the majestic spiritual authority of a Buddha; because he has perfected indestructible wisdom, he is equal toward the three periods of time; and because of the Dharma-body of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra purifies the realm of the single mind.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, having heard of the virtues and conduct of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra from the Tathāgata, cultivated the ten samādhis of a bodhisattva and vowed to behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, seeking him with diligent reflection.
Samantavakṣa Bodhisattva and the entire assembly could not see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva at all.
Then, Samantavakṣa Bodhisattva arose from his meditative absorption and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have entered into ten thousand countless thousands of samādhis, yet I do not see the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s body, speech, or mind, nor his location; furthermore, I do not perceive the ground where he dwells or travels."
The Buddha told Samantadarśin: "It is so, it is so!
You do not see the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra."
Why is this? Because they have already trained in the inexhaustible stages of bodhisattva practice.
Furthermore, Equal Eyes!
Regarding this discourse on the illusory nature of letters through clear wisdom, could one possibly differentiate the illusory forms of wisdom? He replied: "No."
“World-Honored One!
A magical illusion cannot be distinguished by location;
how much less so, then, for the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra!”
In the conduct of body, speech, and mind, where can one find an entry point? Why is this so?
It is because he is endowed with profound and inconceivable virtues, and because his immeasurable explications are inexhaustible; thus, he has attained mastery over adamantine wisdom.
To state the essential point: they thoroughly understand the nature and realm of immeasurable dharmas, remaining unattached to any buddha-field;
regarding all bodies, they comprehend their practice as being without substance, without entry, and as the equality of non-existence.

I possess the domain of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), yet I do not destroy the boundaries of any abiding states; I have no attachment to wealth, for through supernormal knowledge I understand that all things are fundamentally non-existent.
O sons of noble family!

Those who wish to see Samantabhadra Bodhisattva encounter no obstruction in hearing his name, no obstruction in paying him homage, no obstruction in mental reverence, no obstruction in forming the thought of him, no obstruction in approaching him, no obstruction in beholding him, no obstruction in practicing and entering his path, and no obstruction in seeking him; for regarding the vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, they are free from all bonds and hindrances.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin and the assembly of bodhisattvas all longed to behold the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra; together they joined their palms above their heads and spoke these words:
"We take refuge in all Buddhas; we take refuge in Samantabhadra."
Thus he spoke three times.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Samantadarśin, saying:
"You should observe this great assembly of bodhisattvas."
I charge you: you should entreat the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra!
Turn toward all directions with your clear vision, seeking Samantabhadra within your own body;
through the fundamental nature of all dharmas, enter meditative absorption and realize that dharmas are free from desire.
One should, with single-mindedness, direct oneself toward Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
one should understand the limit of primordial non-existence, and by means of the self of the body, establish oneself in all lands;
one should discern the various faculties and cause them to reach everywhere, forever attaining the state of Samantabhadra.
"One who practices in this manner shall behold Samantabhadra.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin and the great assembly, having heard this from the World-Honored One, immediately prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and all together entreated Samantabhadra.

While he was thus making his request, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva manifested a miraculous response, causing the entire assembly to behold Samantabhadra seated upon a great lotus flower to the left and right of the World-Honored One’s feet.
All the bodhisattvas in this assembly appear within his body;

there is no land where they are not seen. As the Buddhas throughout all lands come and go, they see one another in succession, and the voices of these Buddhas proclaim the wisdom of the three periods of time.
At that time, Samantadarśin and the assembly of bodhisattvas, seeing these transformations, were all filled with joy and delight, and together they paid homage to Samantabhadra.

Then, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the merit accumulated by Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, a rain of various flowers fell in profusion; celestial necklaces and lutes resounded in harmony; a rain of fragrant moisture fell, pervading all Buddha-realms; from the midst of the void came the sound of celestial kalavinka birds; and the three evil realms were simultaneously brought to rest.

At that moment, the assembly of immeasurable and immensely liberated bodhisattvas all fully understood the various virtuous practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Then, the Bodhisattva Equal-Eye addressed the Buddha, saying: “These virtues of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva are immeasurable and beyond the reach of limited practice;

they are practices beyond description; they are uninterrupted practices; they are non-reverting practices; they are universally flowing practices; they are practices that reach everywhere without exception; they are non-returning practices; they are practices that discern all dharmas yet are clearly non-discriminatory, following all skillful means; and they are practices that transcend verbal expression.”
The World-Honored One said:
"So it is, Samantacakṣus!"
It is as you have said.

Samantabhadra Bodhisattva purifies countless sentient beings; with infinite purity and immeasurable merit, he generates countless blessings, cultivates countless marks, and possesses boundless virtue. His conduct is peerless, and his fame spreads far and wide.
The practice of non-attainment universally benefits the three periods of time; the renown of the Buddha spreads everywhere and becomes established.
Such are the deeds of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
Chapter Two: The Exposition on the Practice of Concentration Spoken by the Bodhisattva Samanetrin. At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:

"To fulfill the aspirations of the Bodhisattva Equal-Eyed and others, and to clarify the bodhisattva-fields for all bodhisattvas, I shall now expound the ten methods of concentration for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the fundamental practices and merits of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, and the conduct that should be cultivated by all."
What are the ten?
First is attaining the illumination of the primordial great virtue, which is the skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Second is the practice of joyfully inclining toward great meditative concentration, which is the attainment of the skillful means of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Third is the purity of all buddha-fields;
fourth is the purity of cultivating the internal nature;
fifth is the purity of the treasury of the past.
Sixth, Illuminating Treasury of Wisdom;
seventh, Pure Sound of the Buddhas’ Wisdom Resonating Throughout All Buddha-lands;
eighth, Attaining Sovereignty by Discerning the Dharma-realm of the Physical Actions of All Sentient Beings.
The ninth is named attaining the practice of unattached vastness;
the tenth is named attaining the skillful means of the great practices of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
These are the ten great samādhis of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, spoken by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—those already spoken, those currently being spoken, and those yet to be spoken.

“Those bodhisattvas who are able to practice the ten concentrations and whose minds enter therein—this is called awakening; this is called perfect awakening; this is called the Tathāgata who maintains the ten powers; this is called the Guide; this is called the Great Teacher; this is called Universal Wisdom; this is called Manifestation; this is called Infinite Practice; this is called Boundless Practice; and this is called the Supreme Guide of the Dharma.”
One who attains this samādhi manifests universally in all Buddha-lands, roaming and sporting with sovereign ease throughout those realms.
They then guide and sustain the realm of sentient beings, so as to reach the entryway for sentient beings;
they act to bring them to the treasury of non-doubt.
It is the essential practice for entering the Dharma-realm;
it is for awakening to the infinite Dharma-realm;
it is for attaining mastery over the practices of all Tathāgatas of the past, future, and present.
To behold the Dharma of all Tathāgatas;
to expound and comprehend the skillful application of all verbal expressions;
and to attain the practice of sounds, syllables, and phrases.
To fulfill the pure conduct of a bodhisattva; to abide in the conduct of the various vows of a bodhisattva.

"Regarding the three periods of time, they clarify the practice of a single moment; they comprehend the practice of non-duality in all things; they are able to expound the teachings of all Buddhas; through skillful means they turn the wheel of Dharma without turning back; and they fully awaken to the essential practices of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
Through the awakening of a single Buddha, one explains the essentials of all Buddhas; this is the essential dharma of all Bodhisattvas.
Awakening to this wisdom, they clearly understand universal knowledge (*sarvajñā*), which is unsurpassed; thus they fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra.
They clarify and sharpen the various practices of Bodhisattva concentration and wisdom, attain all *dhāraṇīs*, and discern the three periods of time.
To behold the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, and to establish all things within the wisdom of universal knowledge—
this is the purification of the various lands of the Bodhisattvas;
this is the beholding of the spheres of activity of the Buddhas.
“A Bodhisattva who attains this essential Dharma possesses great power within the Bodhisattva-dharmadhātu.

By means of these ten concentrations, they manifest boundless virtues; these virtues are like space, having no finite limit. They shine with immeasurable radiance as Kings of the Worldly Dharma, universally attaining infinite wisdom among all sentient beings. They extensively distribute the Ten Powers, clearly manifesting the life of a recluse, cultivating a mind of tranquility, and universally entering into the practice of stillness.”

Possessing great compassion like a lion, he is a man of wisdom and a manifestor of the Dharma-torch; his reputation for all virtues is inexhaustible, and throughout the world he is inconceivable to both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. He has attained mastery of the dharma-realm and dwells in the accumulation of the Dharma;
he understands various teachings and practices of skillful means, and clearly penetrates all spoken sounds and expressions.

One attains the maintenance of the formless and understands the skillful means regarding forms; one attains purity in what is produced and thereby purifies the Buddha-seed. By discerning the equality of all dharmas, one becomes equal to wisdom;

by understanding the gift of Dharma, one enters the skillful means of the eternal. One thoroughly explains the reality that accords with existence, universally transforms others through the path of wisdom, clarifies the internal nature, and is able to universally receive all practices. One establishes various sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and awakens to the path of wisdom.

Regarding the station of the bodhisattva, it is infinite and inexhaustible; one is universally able to manifest all great transformations, clarify the practice of universal wisdom, and awaken through skillful means—this is called the teaching of Samantabhadra.
"This is the detailed exposition of the ten universal practices of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentrations; this is called the essential practice of the bodhisattva.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, having heard and understood this from the Buddha, knew that he should now make his request.
All those bodhisattvas delighted in what the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin bestowed upon them, and he addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O sons of noble family!
There are ten modes of correct reception which constitute the bodhisattva's dharma of non-remainder."
What are the ten? They are:
to give rise to the Buddha-dharma by practicing in accordance with wisdom;
and to transform and deliver sentient beings by entering the practice of wisdom in accordance with it.
They clarify the wisdom-practice of understanding all buddha-lands and sounds;
they possess the wisdom of the dharma-realm;
and they receive the bodhisattva’s wisdom-practice of skillful means.
They enter the wisdom of non-retrogressive bodhisattvas;
they possess the wisdom that observes the skillful means of the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings;
and they possess the wisdom of the skillful means that governs and sustains the power of the mind.
The wisdom that extensively enters into the mental activities of bodhisattvas;
the wisdom of the universal knowledge of all Buddhas that arises from the power of vows.
O son of noble family!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s ten dharmas of total and exhaustive eradication.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are again ten dharmas by which a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva gives rise to immeasurable mind and wisdom.
What are the ten? They are: to clearly understand the realm of sentient beings; to deliver all those who have arisen; to personally realize the arising of the mind;
to transcend all Buddhas; to give rise to countless minds; to revere the virtues of all Buddhas; and to give rise to a mind that nurtures the multitude.
This means that upon beholding the Buddha, one perceives his immeasurability; regarding all that is seen by the eyes, one gives rise to an immeasurable mind.
This means that encountering the sounds through which the various Buddhas enter [the world], one receives deliverance and manifests an innumerable mind.
This refers to the limit of all Buddhas, who, through discernment, encounter the wisdom of their skillful means; this is called the arising of the countless minds of the worthy and holy ones.
It refers to the power of the Tathāgata’s path entering into non-attachment, which constitutes the arising of the countless minds.

This refers to the power of universal wisdom; one should practice with subtlety and excellence, bringing forth the Buddha-dharma through skillful distribution, and giving rise to immeasurable, vast, and expansive conduct.
This refers to the realm of the Buddha, which is the boundless conduct of universal entry, serving to give rise to the conduct of countless luminous minds.
This refers to the Buddha’s eloquence, wherein all internal natures and aspirations are attained and realized; it refers to seeking all Buddha-dharmas by giving rise to countless minds.
It refers to the Tathāgata’s assembly hall, wherein he universally manifests his presence in all places by giving rise to countless minds.
"O son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to ten incalculable states of mind.
Furthermore, O son of good family!"
Furthermore, there are ten virtues by which a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters into the wisdom of meditative concentration.
What are these ten?
First, while correctly receiving [the state of concentration] in the east, he suddenly awakens from it in the south.
Second, he enters meditative absorption in the south and awakens in the east.
Third, he enters meditative absorption in the northeast and awakens in the southwest.
Fourth, he enters meditative concentration in the southwest and awakens in the northeast.
Fifth, he entered meditative absorption in the south and suddenly appeared awakened in the north.
Sixth, while manifesting absorption in the north, he emerged from it and became aware in the south.
Seventh, he entered absorption in the northwest and appeared awakened in the southeast.
Eighth, when entering meditative absorption in the southeast, one awakens in the northwest.
Ninth, while dwelling in meditative absorption below, one suddenly awakens above.
Tenth, while in meditative absorption above, one remains continuously awake below.
"O son of good family!
The bodhisattva mahāsattva enters the wisdom that discerns the ten concentrations of mind.
Furthermore, O son of good family!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of wisdom regarding the skillful means of great samādhi. What are these ten?
O son of noble family!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests the three-thousandfold world system upon a single lotus flower; he perceives his own body seated cross-legged atop that flower, manifesting his form throughout the three-thousandfold world system and manifesting his radiance throughout the three-thousandfold world system.
In each and every direction, he establishes his body, and with each individual body, he enters a trichiliocosm.
Within all those lands, in each of the four continents, he manifests hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas.
Within each and every bodhisattva practice, he manifests billions upon billions of transformations that accord with the means of deliverance.
Within each and every being thus transformed, he further manifests billions upon billions of distinct manifestations, fully perfecting all their faculties.

Within each and every part, they distinguish the various faculties and thereby attain a full billion koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom are non-retrogressive in the Dharma; yet these are neither a single body nor many bodies, neither entering into meditative absorption (samāpatti) nor awakening from it.
“O son of good family!
For example, the body of an Asura King is seven hundred yojanas tall, yet by his supernormal power he can manifest a body six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height.”
Standing upon the great ocean, he manifested his body half-way up, his head level with Mount Sumeru.
The manifested transformation-body was six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in height, yet his original body suffered no diminution whatsoever.
Just as with the essence of the primary king, there is likewise no doubt regarding the body composed of the four great elements.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the great body as if it were another's body, and not conceive of one's own body as coming to an end.
With the body by which he reigns as king, it is consistently serene;
taking transformation as his joy, transformation becomes his vast power;
through his sovereign capacity for transformation, that which he manifests is beyond doubt and likewise free from delusion.

Those asuras harbor the defilements and poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as various impurities; they give rise to perversity and arrogance, dwelling within the great ocean in their palaces. Yet they are able to manifest such emanation bodies—how much more so, then, for bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas!
One who clearly understands the essential nature of all phenomena as illusory transformations clearly perceives that everything in the world is like a dream!
Knowing the arising of all Buddhas and penetrating the entire universe, one fully comprehends them all to be likewise like transformations.
One understands that all sounds are like echoes!
One contemplates all phenomena and accords with them in their transcendence;
furthermore, just as the Dharma-body is fundamentally pure, so too is the realization of entering into all phenomena!

Clearly understanding that body and mind are vast and devoid of anything substantial, one comprehends the places where countless bodies enter; all these manifest as Buddhas, practicing the Way with purity. How could there be any doubt for those who dwell in this great samādhi?
How much more so when one is deluded?
How could one possibly hear it?
"When one's practice is such as this, one reaches the field of great concentration; appearing in the world to manifest the body, that body enters into all worlds."
Just as that water deity stands in its original position and, by virtue of the body it has received, manifests a great form;
even so, son of good family!
A bhikṣu contemplates the impurity of the body both internally and externally, and likewise contemplates that form and consciousness are entirely like this, practicing with diligent effort.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise: by contemplating the Dharma-body, he establishes manifest practice; whatever he enters, he perceives all of the world and also sees the worldly dharmas, yet regarding those worldly dharmas, he remains pure and without attachment.
This is the realm that moves the bodhisattva, for by virtue of this great being having attained right concentration.
O son of good family!
O bodhisattva mahāsattva!
He enters into all worlds, yet remains unmoved by those worlds.
Chapter Three: The Supernatural Transformations of the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus. "Furthermore, son of good family!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva manifests as many three-thousandfold world systems as there are motes of dust; into each mote of dust he enters and manifests his body;
within each body he manifests a light that shines everywhere;
and within each light he manifests a multitude of forms and images.
Furthermore, each and every mark manifests its full expression;
each and every expression manifests the transformation of sentient beings.

Regarding both these and those, the Bodhisattva fully knows all that exists within the various lands; they understand the desires and attachments of the lands, clarify the purity of the lands, and are skilled in entering them. They know the locations of the lands, comprehend where they abide, clearly understand all lands, and know the activities of all lands.
Just as the Bodhisattva enters into earth, so does he enter into suchness; just as earth is, so does the Bodhisattva enter into suchness.
He does not manifest birth by conceiving of earth, nor does he disparage earth by means of the fundamental nature of dharmas.

“Suppose, noble son, when the sun is about to rise, its light first shines upon the mountains of the seven treasures that encircle Mount Sumeru. Its radiance then penetrates through the intervals between those seven mountains; as the sun’s heat grows more intense, the golden essence of the mountains reflects this light back and forth, shimmering and sparkling brilliantly.”
When the sun moves and shines, all successive realms are fully illuminated; the sun’s palace is universally bright and clear.
Furthermore, the sun’s palace has no limits and encounters no obstructions; it does not think of what it illuminates, nor is there anything it illuminates.
Moreover, the light of the sun does not adhere to the mountains, yet it does not leave the mountains; that which is the brightness of the sun is neither within space, nor is it separate from space.
“In this way, son of good family!

By means of this illumination, when people universally abide equally in the Great Samādhi, whether for a brief moment, a single day and night, a half-month, a month, a year, a hundred years, or throughout the rise and fall of kalpas—whether they possess attachment or are free from it, and whether their state is expansive or narrow, coarse or subtle—they rejoice in the presence of a Buddha’s world and the assembly of Bodhisattvas!”

When encountering a Buddha, all the Buddha-lands where one dwells are pure; in all such abodes, there are various kinds of practices, universal and innumerable assemblies, and immeasurable, inconceivable cycles of birth and death.

There are views of coming and going, views of no coming and going, and various kinds of jewels, up to immeasurable jewels; there are various karmas and various retributions for those karmas, as well as those who should be pure persons.

In that land, he universally contemplates all lands; whatever lands there may be, extending to the limits of all realms of beings, this bodhisattva manifests them all completely, entering into and manifesting them all, traversing them and teaching therein.
"In this way, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, he does not conceive of a dwelling place within any lands;
nor does he depart from the fundamental nature of phenomena regarding all dharmas."
Nor does he enter into the earth;
nor is there any person for whom he forms conceptions.

That bodhisattva does not conceive of anything outside the buddha-field, does not conceive of the existence of the land, does not conceive of the non-existence of the land, and does not destroy the conception of the land.
Nor does he disparage anything.
Furthermore, regarding all phenomena, that bodhisattva does not conceive the notion of unity, nor the notion of difference;
he neither seeks after phenomena nor disparages phenomena.
He fully realizes that the Dharma-realm is fundamentally non-existent.
Chapter Four: The Chapter on the Illusory Deeds of the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus. "For example, son of good family!..."
The name of the illusionist is Śakra’s father.

Regarding the practices of Śakra’s realm, if there is one who has skillfully trained in this illusion and mastered its arts, they can manifest the great illusory feats of Śakra’s father within the four paths of illusion.
The entire multitude remained present and gazed upon it together; all the devas gathered in one place, manifesting one day, seven days, half a month, one month, one year, and a hundred years.
They further manifested cities, walled towns, counties, and villages;
they further manifested rivers, lakes, deep pools, oceans, and flowing streams, as well as rising clouds and falling rain, performing these great transformations.
They manifest the adornment of all lands, yet they do not contend with or disparage the passing of time through these manifestations.
These manifested illusions give rise to celestial joy, yet the illusory substance itself suffers no diminution;
when the devas behold them, they likewise feel neither doubt nor wonder.

These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having entered into meditative absorption through this great samādhi, manifest countless lands within a single land, complete with their respective great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.

Like the jewel mountains of the ocean, Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains—all within the realm of humans, including cities, walls, districts, towns, and various villages—were like celestial palaces.

He clearly comprehends all the palaces of the various nāgas, the abodes of the multitudes of devas, the dwellings of the gandharvas, the haunts of the water-deities, the destinations of the goitrous spirits (galagaṇḍa), the delights of the musicians (kinnara), and the peaceful retreats of the tranquil deities;
furthermore, he understands all the palaces of the world’s extremities, from the desire realm and the form realm up to the formless realm;

and moreover, within the small chiliocosms, the medium dichiliocosms, and the great trichiliocosms, he fully penetrates the births and deaths through which all classes of beings—whether possessing merit or lacking it—undergo their transformations.
Regarding those recollections, they enter them with clear wisdom, seeing thoroughly yet without seeing;
they experience no weariness in all buddha-fields, having abandoned the weariness of this field, they possess no such weariness.
One abandons all practices of the stages; there are neither stages nor practices.
Why is this? Because one has entered into the Dharma by means of subduing [the mind].
Furthermore, that bodhisattva enters into non-attachment toward all phenomena;
regarding the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), they do not conceive of thoughts, as it is empty and has no sphere of activity;
regarding all buddha-fields, they do not conceive of practicing emptiness.

Regarding all embodied existences, there is likewise no life-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*); when one perceives all phenomena through their causes and conditions as they truly are, there is also no life-principle (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
Regarding all arising and ceasing, one transforms through the Dharma;
regarding transformation as non-transformation, the Bodhisattva enters by means of the Dharma through the fulfillment of vows.
The Bodhisattva practices tranquility because all phenomena are still;
the Bodhisattva practices transformation because they do not conceptualize transformation;
they universally deliver sentient beings because they are equal to the purity of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
The Bodhisattva’s practice within the dharma-realm is inconceivable, for dharmas are without grasping;
the Bodhisattva practices compassion, universally employing skillful means to transform sentient beings.
Thus, while the Bodhisattva dwells in a single land, they clearly perceive the dwelling places and spheres of activity within countless lands.
They comprehend the bodily conduct of countless classes of sentient beings;

they manifest the cultivation and establishment of countless bodhisattvas; they keep in mind the arising and manifestation of countless Buddhas; and they receive the teachings on the essential principles of the equal, perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas.
"Practicing the bodhisattva path there,
they vanish here and appear there;
vanishing there, they suddenly appear here."
Practicing without disparaging me, one enters the Dharma-realm; clearly entering into tranquility, one recollects wisdom to benefit those in darkness.
Just as a magician stands upon this ground and manifests illusions, yet the manifestation of these illusions does not damage the ground, for the illusory phenomena manifested depend upon that ground.
An illusion does not conceive of day and night, nor does it destroy the seasons!
In this same way, the Bodhisattva enters into lands by means of the absence of a realm of lands;
he clearly understands lands by means of the absence of a land.
Furthermore, one uses the concept of a land to clarify the absence of a land;
one manifests as dwelling in form while being in the realm of formlessness.
One does not negate duality by means of unity.
Nor does one disparage the one by means of the two.
For example, one who is named "Illusion" understands the dharmas of all lands; entering into the illusion of dharmas, they clarify their entry into the illusion of wisdom;
having entered the illusion of wisdom, they understand their entry into the illusion of practice.
Having entered into the illusion of conditioned phenomena, one gives rise to the illusion of wisdom; and by means of this illusory wisdom, one discerns all conditioned phenomena.
Just as that illusory person does not manifest his illusion outside of the ground, nor does he exist apart from the crowd of onlookers.
So it is with the Bodhisattva!
He does not enter the various lands by means of empty space,
nor does he enter empty space from outside the lands.
Why is this? Because the land enters into empty space without being destroyed; thus, one who can enter the realm of the land enters empty space.
This is how that Bodhisattva universally adorns and arrays [the land], entering into all practices through the textual descriptions of the realms of the land.
With equal vision and no views, they bring about non-destruction; cultivating clear understanding and insight, they practice and observe.
In the space of a single finger-snap, they pervade countless lands and fully comprehend all that is born.
Regarding the passing of eons upon eons, that which can be practiced in a single moment exceeds that number across immeasurable eons.
This passing of eons is such that the accumulated [karmic] formations have ceased to exist, leaving nothing but thought.
In the space of a single finger-snap, he manifests vast deeds without relying on mental intention, for he delights in the illusion of wisdom.
This bodhisattva studies the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) so as to transcend the illusion of wisdom, penetrate the illusion of the world, and clearly surpass the illusion of dharmas.
He dwells without conflict amidst the illusions of the world, universally practicing the conduct of wisdom. His illusory power transcends the three periods of time and passes beyond the incalculable.

His illusory power surpasses that of the penetrating wisdoms, entering into the illusion of the mind; it exceeds billions of limits, surpassing the illusions of all Buddhas, and universally delivers beings to the infinite.
So it is with the Bodhisattva!
They understand and enter all lands, comprehending them all completely, yet they are forever without attachment and entirely without conceptual thought.
They are like that illusory person!
By means of the illusion of the celestial net, all illusions are universally manifested; yet one does not abide within illusion, nor is there any delusion.
Such is the Bodhisattva!
This is the attainment of entry into the *pāramitā* of all dharmas!
Not dwelling on entering the Dharma, yet entering the Dharma without confusion—this is what is called the Bodhisattva’s "Vast and Universal Great Samādhi.
Chapter Five: The Bodhisattva’s Joyful Samādhi. Furthermore, sons of good family!
O Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantacakṣus!
To the east of here, passing beyond incalculable Buddha-fields,
there is a land named Paramapāramitā.
In that realm there is a meditative absorption called the Unsurpassed Perfection (anuttara-pāramitā).
Just as in the land from which he has departed, he attains the most supreme land.
In that land, there may be lands where this absorption is attained at the early hour, the midday hour, the afternoon hour, the western hour, or the late evening hour.
Whether for the duration of a single thought-moment, a brief instant, or a season;
whether for five nights, fifteen days, one month, or even one year; whether for a hundred years, a thousand years;
or for ten million years, a hundred million years, a hundred billion years, or a hundred trillion *nayuta* years.

Whether for the duration of one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, or a thousand kalpas, or a hundred thousand kalpas, or ten million billion nayutas of kalpas, or incalculable kalpas, or immeasurable kalpas, or boundless kalpas, or again infinite kalpas, or inexhaustible kalpas, or inconceivable kalpas, or infinite kalpas as vast as space, or infinite thought-moments of kalpas, or immeasurable kalpas that exceed all measure.
Yet that bodhisattva does not form a conceptual desire for dwelling because of the time of the Dharma;
nor does he form a conceptual desire for dwelling because of the seasons.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not give rise to thoughts of weariness because of various times;
nor does he give rise to such thoughts therein.

There is neither dualistic practice, nor the notion of "I act," nor thought, nor the absence of thought, nor the perception of thought; there is no thought of sitting in meditative concentration, nor the thought of arising from it, because all dharmas are limitless.
For example, it is like the Sun Deity who illuminates the paths for all the devas.

The sun moves along its course, yet the devas neither follow nor cease from their own movement; the sun does not emerge at night, nor does it think of day. Only when the sun has already set each day do they realize it.
Nor is it known by those gods, nor does it perish during the night.
In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having mastered this samādhi, enters meditative absorption in countless lands without any perception of time,
nor does he have any conceptual thoughts.
This, noble son, is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s samādhi of the supreme perfection of the land; it is the practice of unsurpassed and incomparable skillful wisdom.
Chapter Six: The Great Power, Wisdom, and Samādhi of the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin "Furthermore, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva understands with equanimity the bodies of all sentient beings and the body of the Buddha."
By means of this, he extensively contemplates the Tathāgatas in countless lands as numerous as motes of dust;
he makes offerings to all those Tathāgatas with every kind of flower and every supreme worldly jewel.
They made offerings of all manner of jewels, scattering them upon him;
they made offerings of all kinds of ornaments and various places for walking meditation.

They constructed stupas and monasteries using countless *maṇi* gems as an offering. These offerings surpassed anything created by the gods; that such offerings were made was entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha.
All Buddha-lands are pure, and all manner of offerings are received through the Buddha’s mindful assistance; by making these offerings to this Buddha, one also makes offerings to all Buddhas.

He prostrated at the feet of those Tathāgatas, offering his entire physical form as an act of worship; with profound reverence, he inquired about the Buddhas' teachings, wishing for them to expound the equal Dharma of all Buddhas, to propagate the Great Dharma of all Buddhas, and to enter the essential practices of all Buddhas.
Practicing great compassion, they enter into infinite powers of harmonious conduct and equality; they contemplate the Buddhas entering into the essential needs of all sentient beings.
They clearly enter into the fundamental accumulation [of merit and wisdom], yet they do not perceive the arising of a Buddha, nor do they notice the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgatas.
Just as when the mind gives rise to a thought, one does not know whence it arises, nor where it returns;
so too, the Bodhisattva does not perceive the arising of the Tathāgata, nor does he perceive the cessation of the Tathāgata.
"Just as, during the daytime, a mirage-river does not arise from the shadows,
nor does it emerge from that spring,
nor does it abide upon the earth;
Nor does it come from the eastern peak;
it is neither existent nor non-existent;
it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
It is neither clear nor turbid; it cannot be drunk, nor can it be defiled; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it has no flavor, nor can it be tasted.
Material forms are like reflections in water; based upon them, thoughts arise.
Like a mirage that appears as a river, one then has the perception of a river.
By departing from such perceptions, one distances oneself from the near and remains unharmed.
The River of Wild Horses (Yema) is likewise unfit for habitation.
It is the same with the Bodhisattva:

they do not give rise to [the notion of] the Tathāgatas, nor do they perceive the arising of the Tathāgatas, nor do they perceive the passing away of the Tathāgatas; it is only because of the perception of marks that they conceive of the Buddhas as existing!
By means of signlessness, they are without conceptualization.
"O sons of noble family!
O bodhisattva mahāsattvas!"
It is called the Samādhi of Purity.
By means of this samādhi, one enters meditative absorption and awakens from it without losing that concentration.
It is like a person of clear intelligence who, while sleeping and dreaming, knows that all actions within the dream are without causal basis, and upon awakening, recognizes them as such.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva likewise beholds all Buddhas while forgetting his own consciousness.

He upholds the teachings of all Buddhas, knows the sites where all Tathāgatas sit in assembly, brings about the supreme purification of all Buddha-fields, understands their meanings and principles, clearly discerns the essentials of all dharmas, extensively reveals the causes and conditions of all dharmas, manifests and benefits the lineage of the Buddhas, practices the pure majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas, and widely expounds the eloquence of all Buddhas.
O son of good family!
This is the skillful wisdom of the great samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Chapter Seven: The Immeasurable Suchness of the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus. "Furthermore, O son of good family!"

The practice of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva involves recollecting the past Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, and their boundless emergence for the sake of deliverance, extending through kalpa after kalpa and across all lands to the furthest reaches of infinity.

One should clearly know that throughout all lands, for kalpas beyond kalpas, there shall be the arising of all Buddhas; one should clearly know that throughout all kalpas, for kalpas beyond kalpas, they shall arise.

One should understand that as all Buddhas arise and expound the sutras, they practice the *pāramitā* of deliverance; from kalpa to kalpa, they preach the Dharma and practice the *pāramitā* of deliverance.

They possess the *pāramitā* of knowing the mental formations; they possess the *pāramitā* of knowing all feelings. Within the *pāramitā* of feelings, they know the various kinds of mental formations, and thereby clearly understand the various lifespans of the Tathāgatas.
They know both this and that regarding all lifespans, even those exceeding billions of *nayutas* of years; they know both this and that.
Practicing with this wisdom, they know that the noble conduct of immeasurable Tathāgatas is fundamentally immeasurable;
they clearly know that the various lands of the past are fundamentally immeasurable;
and they clearly know that the various kalpas of the past are fundamentally immeasurable.
Just as one knows that the past dharmas are originally non-existent and immeasurable;
just as one knows that the past mind is originally non-existent and immeasurable;
just as one knows that the past liberation is originally non-existent and immeasurable.
Just as one knows that the past actions of sentient beings were originally non-existent and immeasurable;
just as one knows that what was spoken in the past was originally non-existent and immeasurable;
just as one knows that the arising in the past was originally non-existent and immeasurable;
As for the meditative absorption through which it is named the "Treasury of Transcending Adornments":
by giving rise to a single thought-moment, one can transcend hundreds of thousands of kalpas of fundamental non-existence and the immeasurable.

With a mind that has passed through more than a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, further through incalculable kalpas, further through inconceivable kalpas, further through immeasurable kalpas, further through boundless kalpas, further through limitless kalpas, further through asaṃkhyeya kalpas, further through inconceivable kalpas, and further through kalpas beyond all hope—indeed, passing even beyond kalpas beyond all hope—the causal conditions thereof do not cease. Having attained the fixed meditative absorption (samādhi) without any cause from the past, he establishes ten dharmas as that very concentration.
Furthermore, there is another awakening, which also establishes ten dharmas.
Regarding all Tathāgatas, one attains entry into the inconceivable, arising in purity;
nor is there any dwelling in cultivation or establishment.
Having attained it, one supervises and brings it forth; receiving it in full, one maintains it with reverence, seeking equality and entering the three spheres.
What are the ten?
First, understanding and comprehending the conduct of fundamental ignorance.
Second, the inexhaustible dharma of eloquent exposition;
third, the discernment of non-destruction and non-contention;
fourth, the discernment of non-abiding.
Fifth, his eloquence is unshakable.
Sixth, that which he has spoken is sincere and truthful.
Seventh, he serves as a refuge and dwelling place for all.
Eighth, to be inclined toward the three realms with joy.
Ninth, to be the supreme foundation for all virtues.
Tenth, to be free from contempt or arrogance regarding all phenomena.
“O son of good family!
These are the ten practices of no-limitation, which are realized through these ten certainties.
For example, O son of good family!”

When one is within the womb and is about to be born, the consciousness has already entered; at that very moment, the Bodhisattva likewise awakens from meditative concentration and flows into the Dharma by means of these ten.
At that time, O son of good family!
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the purity of the past.

Chapter Eight: The Purity of Expedient Wisdom. **Chapter Eight: The Purity of Expedient Wisdom** [The Buddha said: "Furthermore, son of good family, what is meant by the purity of expedient wisdom? It refers to the bodhisattva’s skillful application of means to manifest various forms of birth. That is to say, he may manifest birth among the gods, or manifest birth among humans, or manifest birth among the various classes of asuras, or manifest birth among the various classes of yakṣas, or manifest birth among the various classes of gandharvas, or manifest birth among the various classes of kumbhāṇḍas, or manifest birth among the various classes of piśācas, or manifest birth among the various classes of mahoragas, or manifest birth among the various classes of nāgas, or manifest birth among the various classes of pretas, or manifest birth among the various classes of animals, or manifest birth among the various classes of hell-beings.

In this way, the bodhisattva manifests birth within all the various destinies of the six realms of existence. Yet, although he manifests birth within these various destinies, he does not undergo the suffering of those destinies. Why is this? Because the bodhisattva has already transcended the three realms of existence; it is solely for the sake of maturing sentient beings that he manifests birth within the various destinies. Furthermore, the bodhisattva manifests birth within the various destinies by means of the power of his vows and the power of his skillful means. He manifests birth within the various destinies through the power of his vows, yet he is never separated from the power of the Buddhas. He manifests birth within the various destinies through the power of skillful means, yet he is never separated from the true nature of reality (dharmatā). Son of good family, this is called the purity of expedient wisdom."
"Furthermore, son of good family!
Because each and every land is purified, the bodhisattva mahāsattva enters each and every realm;
having already cultivated each and every realm, he manifests within each and every realm."
By upholding each and every land in accordance with reality, one dwells in each and every buddha-field;
having illuminated each and every buddha-field, one understands each and every land, and by traversing each and every land, one thoroughly realizes the purity of each and every land.
In those various lands and throughout all future times, they shall be supreme among men;
in those lands, throughout the succession of kalpas, they shall have something to teach;
and throughout those kalpas, they shall clearly comprehend all manifestations.
They discern all kalpas; they guide others through all kalpas;
and they maintain equanimity throughout all kalpas.
Throughout all kalpas, there is nothing that does not arise;
throughout all kalpas, one practices the immeasurable;
throughout all kalpas, the fragrance is universally sublime.
Throughout all kalpas, there is compassion;
throughout all kalpas, there have been no past Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.
That which is to be spoken in the future may or may not be spoken.
There is that which is granted as a prediction of enlightenment and that which is not granted as a prediction;

there are various distinct names, innumerable names, immeasurable names, limitless names, boundless names, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) names, inconceivable names, shoreless names, and names beyond expectation.

When he shall arise, out of compassion to deliver sentient beings, manifesting as a Dharma King and acting as a guide through his cultivation of practice, he shall universally expound the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and extensively praise all meritorious deeds;
he shall widely propagate and elucidate the practices that bring clear realization;
furthermore, he shall purify his mind and establish his nature and conduct through cultivation.
One should accomplish the practice of all virtues;
one should widely proclaim the supreme and essential practices;
and furthermore, one should establish the discourse of universal wisdom.
One should also transcend the practices of all Tathāgatas;
one should also cultivate and fulfill all vows.
Furthermore, one should practice beyond the perfection of wisdom, clearly understanding and fully realizing the excellence of accomplished virtue.
Furthermore, surpassing the practice of supreme adornment and clarity, he establishes a superior retinue and likewise understands and masters the Dharma;
moreover, he cultivates an understanding of the correspondence between transgressions and blessings;
and furthermore, he cultivates the contemplation of the perfection of the marks of accomplishment.
He clearly understands and realizes the excellence of fulfillment;
he clearly understands and penetrates the virtue of equanimity;
and he also clearly understands the intentions of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
They also know their spiritual lineages and understand their skillful practices;
they also know expedient means, their transformations, and their destinations;
they also know the attainment of Buddhahood, the deliverance of individuals, the deliverance of countless sentient beings, the parinirvāṇa of all Tathāgatas, and the timing of all Buddhas.

At the very moment he resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he clearly understood the events of kalpas— further exceeding hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, hundreds of thousands of kalpas, and billions of kalpas;
he further exceeded kalpas as numerous as the dust motes of Jambudvīpa,
and again exceeded kalpas as numerous as the dust motes of the four continents.
Passing through as many eons as there are motes of dust in a thousand worlds;
passing through as many eons as there are motes of dust in a great trichiliocosm;
passing through as many eons as there are motes of dust in a trichiliocosm of world-systems.

it further passed through eons as numerous as the atoms in the lands of a thousand Buddhas;
it further passed through eons as numerous as the atoms in the lands of a hundred thousand Buddhas.

furthermore, he passed through as many eons as there are atoms in countless buddha-fields;
furthermore, he passed through incalculable eons.
Furthermore, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of immeasurable worlds;
furthermore, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of boundless worlds;
furthermore, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of incalculable worlds.
Again, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of an asaṃkhyeya;
again, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of the inconceivable;
again, he passed through kalpas as numerous as the atoms of the limitless.
Furthermore, they pass through kalpas as numerous as the atoms in infinite joys;
furthermore, they pass through kalpas as numerous as the atoms in joyless joys.

By means of the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the Samādhi of the Treasury of Wisdom-Light, they uphold the teachings of each individual land; likewise, they enter each individual land, and their lineage is as that of each individual land—this is also the case for lands as numerous as the atoms in infinite joys!
Clearly knowing the infinite lands of the future, the bodhisattva, through wisdom and meditative concentration, universally enters into whatever thoughts and intentions arise.
There are ten bases of reliance; what are these ten?
First, it refers to those who contemplate and delight in Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, established by Tathāgatas as many as there are motes of dust;
these bodhisattvas are sustained by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas.
Second, it refers to bodhisattvas who are established in and abide by the Dharma, being clearly proficient in the ten dhāraṇīs within the world.
Having already attained the ten dhāraṇīs and perfected inexhaustible eloquence;
third, the bodhisattva relies on practice, being established by practice, and fulfills their conduct through the ultimate supreme vow.
Fourth, the bodhisattva is established by relying on the power of virtue, such that no one can surpass or excel them.
Fifth, the bodhisattva is established by relying on wisdom, because they are unimpeded in their practice of the Buddha-dharma.
Sixth, the bodhisattva stands upon great compassion and turns the wheel of Dharma because there is no turning back.
Seventh, he stands upon those various practices, for he has skillfully cultivated and established the practice of all dharmas through various syllables and words.
Eighth, the bodhisattva abides by relying on the supreme dharmas that give rise [to awakening], opening the gate of ambrosia and closing the gates of all evils.
Ninth, the bodhisattva abides by relying on the power of wisdom, practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva without interruption.

Tenth, that bodhisattva establishes himself by relying on the power of equanimity and fulfills the power of generosity; having delivered countless beings, he causes them to practice the immeasurable powers upon which bodhisattvas rely, thereby clearly understanding infinite eons.

“The Bodhisattva attains [this] by relying on the power of the Dharma; because all dharmas are fundamentally pure and because all that arises is infinite, this is called the sixth supreme practice of the great wisdom-concentration of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.”
“Abiding in this, that bodhisattva attains a thorough understanding of the practices throughout infinite eons;
clearly discerns the expedient practices throughout infinite eons;
and thoroughly understands the characteristics of the expedient practices performed by infinite numbers of sentient beings.”
Having attained mastery through the discernment of infinite modes of both sinful and meritorious conduct, one gains the skillful means of expedient action;
furthermore, regarding the infinite modes of diligence practiced, one manifests entry among sentient beings through the skillful means of acting while being without action;
and within this acting without action, there are infinite skillful modes of action regarding both the good and the evil.
In the practice of non-practice, one understands and masters the provisional practice of all dharmas;

in the practice of non-practice, regarding the arising of Buddhas at various times, according to their forms, their teachings, and their modes of arising and ceasing, one understands the provisional practice of the lineage of all Buddhas;
in the practice of non-practice, one explains the gates of immeasurable wisdom, which is the provisional practice of turning back [the flow of existence].
In practicing non-practice, universal wisdom is stirred; through countless transformations, he manifests expedient practices according to the time.
"For example, noble son!

When the sun rises, a person with sight can see, one after another, the various provinces, kingdoms, counties, towns, and villages; they also know the high and low elevations, mountains, rivers, and rugged valleys; they know the various species of trees and grains; they know what is beautiful and what is ugly;
they also know what is pure and what is impure;
and they likewise know everything that exists in the world.
One with clear vision and penetrating understanding should contemplate this with a discerning mind. Noble son!
Just as the sun’s radiance is without distinction, yet its bright illumination allows those who possess eyes to perceive all forms through its pervasive light.
"In this way, son of good family!

That bodhisattva has already attained the samādhi of non-differentiation and clearly understands all conditioned activities and non-activities, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas.
He knows their seeds and grains; he clarifies them and recognizes them. By means of such clarity and ten kinds of non-delusion, he fulfills all sentient beings throughout the ten directions."
What are the ten?
First, manifesting before sentient beings without confusing their roots of virtue.
Second, transforming and delivering sentient beings without confusion.
Third, they deliver sentient beings from states of delusion.

Fourth, they are without delusion regarding the practices undertaken for the sake of sentient beings; they act according to what is appropriate and speak according to what is true, bringing all discourses to ultimate completion.
Fifth, their conduct is free from delusion, and they are pure in all lands.
Sixth, their entries are free from delusion; they practice without practicing in all Buddha-lands, and by practicing without practicing, they resolve the doubts of sentient beings.
Seventh, there is no delusion regarding one's vows; as requested, one carries out the practice of delivering sentient beings and fulfills all aspirations.
Eighth, there is no delusion regarding the methods of skillful means, which are without limit or obstruction, being the gateway to pure wisdom.

Ninth, preaching the Dharma without delusion, one can rain down the universal Dharma, leaving no passions uncontrolled; through non-action within action, and through the practice of universal wisdom, one causes others to establish themselves in the Buddha-way.

Tenth, O Bodhisattva! The great responsibility of wisdom free from delusion is boundless; the practice of the gateway of pure wisdom is unerring; it manifests without darkness, illuminating the entire world with clarity.
Having already abided in the ten practices free from delusion and having already abided in this samādhi, the bodhisattva soon arose from that concentration;
he was venerated by the lords of the devas, honored by the lords of the nāgas who rained down exquisite incense,
and received the respectful salutations of the lords of the spirits.
He is honored and revered by all the Śakra-devānām-indras;
he is sought after and turned toward by all the Garuḍa-devas and spirits;
and he is entreated with prostrations by all the Brahmā-devas.
He was praised and extolled by the Sovereign Deity of All Joyful Spirits;
he was lauded by the Sovereign Deity of Tranquility;
and he was sought after by the Sovereign Deities of All Fragrances.
He is honored and supported by all the lords of men.
O son of noble family!
This is the sixth manifestation of the practice of great wisdom and skillful means, known as the Samādhi of the Treasury of Wisdom-Light for all Bodhisattvas.

Chapter Nine: The Manifestation of the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin Furthermore, son of good family, there is a samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattva called "The Manifestation of All Buddhas and the Purity of Their Lands."
"What do you think, son of good family!
How do the bodhisattvas and buddhas clearly manifest and enter into meditative absorption in the pure lands?
In this regard, a bodhisattva enters the worlds of the eastern direction, proceeding from one land to another."
In the southwest, north, and the four intermediate directions, as well as above and below, he likewise travels from one land to another.
In those various lands, he universally manifests the performance of Buddha-works:

before all Tathāgatas, he manifests the Buddha’s stirring of compassion, the Buddha’s enjoyment, the Buddha’s manifestation of majesty, the Buddha’s realm, the Buddha’s sovereignty, the Buddha’s lion’s roar, the Buddha’s various practices, the Buddha’s adornments, the Buddha’s supernormal powers, the assemblies of all Buddhas, the purity of the assemblies, the equality of the assemblies, the unity of the assemblies, the greatness of the assemblies, the reliance of the assemblies, the resting places of the assemblies, the teaching and transforming of the assemblies, the assemblies according to their needs, the heroic grandeur of the assemblies, and the assemblies of the Jambudvīpa multitudes.
The four regions are likewise;
the thousand lands are likewise;
and the two-thousand lands are likewise.
It is likewise in the trichiliocosm.

He manifests the assembly grounds throughout billions, nayutas, and hundreds of thousands of lands; he manifests the assembly grounds in incalculable lands; he manifests the assembly grounds in as many lands as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields;
to state it briefly, he universally manifests the assembly grounds in as many lands as there are atoms in countless and immeasurable Buddha-fields.

“In that assembly, he manifests the various visions of all Buddhas; he manifests the various physical forms of all Buddhas; he manifests the various times of all Buddhas; he manifests the various places of all Buddhas; he manifests the various transformations of all Buddhas; he manifests the various inspirations of all Buddhas; he manifests the various adornments of all Buddhas; he manifests the various dignified demeanors of all Buddhas; he manifests the various physical appearances of all Buddhas; and he manifests the various deeds of all Buddhas.”
"In those various assemblies, the bodhisattva sees himself present everywhere;
he also sees himself there, universally preaching the sutras;
and he also sees himself universally upholding all dharmas."
Furthermore, they know for themselves that they possess the skillful means regarding all phenomena;
they know for themselves that they understand all principles and meanings;
and they know for themselves that they have attained mastery over emptiness.
They also know for themselves that they have clearly realized the Dharma-body;
they also know for themselves and are without fear or timidity;
they also know for themselves that they do not abide in permanence.
He also knows for himself that he does not dwell in conceptual perceptions;
he also knows for himself that he is free from the perception of weariness;
and he also knows for himself that he has clearly understood all forms of wisdom.
He also knows and understands all meanings for himself;
he also knows and reflects upon the stages of all conditioned phenomena for himself;
he also knows and realizes the meaning of equanimity for himself.
He also knows for himself that there is nothing further to be thought;
he also knows for himself that he is single-mindedly mindful of all Buddhas;
he also knows for himself that he is equanimously mindful of all powers.
He also knows for himself that he maintains equanimity toward all sensory perceptions;
he also knows for himself that he maintains equanimity toward the practice of emptiness;
and he also knows for himself that he maintains equanimity toward seclusion and tranquility.
Knowing this, one does not dwell on the land, nor does one dwell on persons;
nor does one dwell on the meaning of the Buddha,
nor does one construct dharmas.
Neither does one destroy the body;
nor does one destroy bodily conduct;
nor does one engage in mental ideation.
Nor does it enter into mental activity;
nor does one conceive of a life span;
nor does one conceive of a self, a person, or a location.
For example, it is like knowing the Dharma through the Dharma, neither giving rise to the bodhisattva practice of existence or non-existence;
there is no recollection, nor does one recollect wandering through various lands.
"He can manifest countless forms and images of the Buddha, fulfill all practices, and being able to practice with equal purity, he attains that state."
They are able to fully manifest the physical forms and marks of a Buddha, as well as all the radiance of a Buddha.
These manifestations are impartial and surpassingly pure; through their ascent, they are fully revealed.
They are able to manifest forms identical to those of a Buddha’s image; they manifest light identical to that of a Buddha;
they also manifest mental images identical to those of a Buddha;
and they also manifest the infinite marks and embellishments of a Buddha’s body.
They also manifest the Buddha’s supreme majestic spiritual brilliance;
they also manifest the Buddha’s supreme excellence of physical marks;
they also manifest the Buddha’s body in the color of adamant.
They also manifest the pure-colored forms of the Buddha-body;
they also manifest the immeasurable-colored forms of the Buddha-body;
they also manifest the forms of the great clear maṇi-jewel of the Buddha-body.
They also manifest the body of the Tathāgata as having seven blades;
they also manifest the body of the Tathāgata as having eight blades;
they also manifest the body of the Tathāgata as having nine blades.
They also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as ten blades;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as twenty blades;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as thirty blades.
He also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as forty blades;
he also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as fifty blades;
he also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as sixty blades.
They also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like seventy blades;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like eighty blades;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like ninety blades.
They also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like a hundred blades;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like ten *li*;
and they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as being like half a *yojana*.
They also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as one yojana;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as ten yojanas;
they also manifest the body of a Tathāgata as a hundred yojanas.
He also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a thousand yojanas;
he also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as one Jambudvīpa;
and he also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as the four continents.
He also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a thousand worlds;
he also manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a trichiliocosm.
