Or again, he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a hundred Buddha-fields; or again, he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a thousand [Buddha-fields].
Sometimes he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a hundred thousand Buddha-fields;
sometimes he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as a billion nayuta Buddha-fields; sometimes he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as immeasurable Buddha-fields;
sometimes he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as infinite Buddha-fields; or again, he manifests the body of a Tathāgata as vast as [Akṣobhya]...
He may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as many as the *saṃkhyeya* buddha-fields; or again, he may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as many as the boundless (*ananta*) buddha-fields;

or again, he may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as many as the limitless (*aparyanta*) buddha-fields; or again, he may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as many as the inconceivable (*acintya*) buddha-fields;
or again, he may manifest the body of a Tathāgata as many as the inexpressible (*anabhilāpya*) buddha-fields; or again, he may manifest the body of a Tathāgata.
Just as in the Buddha-field of Transcended Thought, or again manifesting the body of a Tathāgata like the Buddha-field of No Place,
or again manifesting the body of a Tathāgata like the Buddha-field of the Inconceivable, or again manifesting the body of a Tathāgata like the Buddha-field of Beyond Hope and Transcending Hope.
In this way, the Bodhisattva manifests the body of that Tathāgata in such a manner, with countless colors and countless marks.
He manifests immeasurable beauty, immeasurable light, and immeasurable nets of radiance.
He manifests that innumerable dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; he manifests that innumerable dharmas are fundamentally devoid of self.
He manifests that all dharmas arise from the source of wisdom; he manifests an inexhaustible body and manifests the purity of non-action.
In this way, O Bodhisattva!
These Tathāgatas manifest, yet within the bodies of those Tathāgatas, there is neither increase nor decrease.

"It is like space, which knows neither weariness nor fatigue, and has neither smallness nor greatness; even in the countless lands and in the depths of darkness within all lands, it does not become dark or vast."
The body of that Tathāgata is also like this!
By means of its vastness, it manifests neither smallness nor greatness.
It is like the reflection of the moon illuminating Jambudvīpa; it has neither smallness nor greatness, and while the reflection of the moon remains, its radiance neither comes nor goes.
It is the same for that bodhisattva!
Having attained this samādhi and dwelling therein as if manifesting a Buddha, they do not falsely destroy the physical form of the Tathāgata; yet the Buddhas thus manifested are merely like a dream!

In this, there is nothing seen, yet there is seeing; and the voices of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas manifest. These manifested voices of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are empty of phenomena and are merely non-existent!
Yet all receive the Dharma and propagate it, remaining entirely within the state of non-delusion.
Just as sentient beings, at the point of death, turn toward their destination with their minds racing,
so too is it with the Bodhisattva!
Abiding thus in samādhi, he adorns all lands, purifying them through the deliverance of the Buddha’s wisdom.
The Bodhisattva responds universally and equally by means of ten rapidities.

What are the ten? They are: swiftly fulfilling and perfecting all vows and practices; swiftly illuminating all lands with the Buddha-dharma; swiftly delivering sentient beings through the wheel of Dharma and skillful wisdom; swiftly purifying all lands in accordance with all appropriate actions; swiftly accomplishing wisdom, the ten powers, and so forth; swiftly achieving equanimity through all Tathāgatas; swiftly desiring to subdue Māra by the power of great compassion; swiftly desiring to gladden sentient beings by severing their doubts; swiftly manifesting and moving those to be saved according to their needs; and swiftly turning toward the Dharma-gates with various sounds to purify all lands.
“Bodhisattvas have ten seals, by which all dharmas seal those bodhisattvas.
What are the ten?
Those bodhisattvas practice the same root of virtue as all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”
Those bodhisattvas are unified into a single body, for the Dharma-body is unsurpassed.
Those bodhisattvas act through a single practice, for the Tathāgata is non-dual.
Those bodhisattvas constitute countless fields, for they arise from non-duality.
That bodhisattva practices boundlessly, for they are equal to the Dharma-body.
That bodhisattva is unimpeded, for they have attained the ten powers within the world.
That bodhisattva practices the pure dharma of emptiness, for their practice is non-dual.
That bodhisattva is untainted, for the sake of the world’s ultimate deliverance.
That bodhisattva has no internal [self], because of universal wisdom, skillful means, and insight.
That bodhisattva is protected, by virtue of all the Buddhas.
"O son of good family!
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva possesses a great wisdom-concentration called 'The Universal Illumination of the Buddha-Lands through the Sounds of All Buddhas.
When that Bodhisattva practices this concentration and enters into meditative absorption (samāpatti), there is no one who can act as his teacher."
One enters the teachings of all Buddhas for the sake of being free from doubt and confusion.
One becomes a man of supreme worldly wisdom for the sake of purity.
The mind is fundamentally pure and luminous for the sake of being most honored and great.
They act as guides for the world because they hold themselves in high esteem;
they give rise to the most fierce and courageous resolve to establish the Buddhas of the future because it is the fundamental seed of universal wisdom;
and they cultivate wisdom to achieve faith because their words are non-dual.
The wisdom of the past is unimpeded because it accomplishes the treasury of the Dharma.
By means of the teachings of all Buddhas, it raises the rain of Dharma according to the conduct of sentient beings as appropriate.
"For example, son of good family!..."
Śakra Devānām Indra, the Heavenly King Maṇiśakra, dwells in the most honored place; his maṇi jewel illuminates with majesty the Heavenly King Śakra.
By virtue of this divine power, whoever obtains this maṇi jewel shall possess the greatest majestic authority as the Heavenly King Śakra.
By ten matters, he attains preeminence among the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
What are these ten?
By virtue of having the most excellent celestial form, he surpasses all other sons of the gods.
Because they most resemble devas,
because they manifest the marks of a deva among the retinue of devas,
and because they possess the supreme desires of a deva.
By means of the supreme bliss of the devas,
by means of the celestial garments of faith,
and by means of the supreme sovereignty of the devas.
By means of celestial intent and celestial great wisdom, through the virtue of this maṇi jewel,
those who obtain it shall attain the state of the Most Honored One among the devas.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Upon attaining this meditative absorption (samādhi-samāpatti), they immediately attain the ten vast and boundless wisdoms.
What are these ten?
That is to say: attaining unimpeded wisdom regarding the Buddha-fields;
attaining the practice of wisdom from the very beginning regarding all sentient beings;
and attaining appropriate wisdom by relying upon the three periods of time.
This refers to attaining the wisdom that serves as the basis for the bodies of all Buddhas;
it refers to attaining the practice of wisdom regarding the teachings of all Buddhas;
and it refers to attaining the practice of wisdom regarding all phenomena as being the one phenomenon.
It refers to the wisdom that attains entry into the dharmakāya, which transcends all worlds;
it refers to the practice of wisdom that has fundamentally attained equality regarding all phenomena;
it refers to the wisdom that serves as the basis for the attainment of all sovereign powers.
This refers to the method for attaining the wisdom that brings joy regarding all phenomena; having attained this samādhi, one purifies the world with the voices of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there are ten matters by which a bodhisattva attains the purity of physical majesty.
What are the ten? They are:
to attain through non-attainment; to practice boundless conduct; and not to dwell in any land.
To hope through hopelessness; and to manifest various forms and images within all lands while abiding in purity.
This means that by means of the aspiration of non-aspiration, one radiates light-fields, dwelling therein to deliver sentient beings.
It means that by means of the perception of non-perception, one dwells within that body, acting to bring forth all Buddhas.
This means that by seeking through the seeking of non-seeking, one rains down countless flowers and incense to make offerings to all Buddhas;
and by mindfulness through the mindfulness of non-mindfulness, one provides various musical offerings to the Buddhas in order to deliver sentient beings.

That is to say, one should make offerings to all Buddhas with unattached attachment, pure multitudes of things, and countless ornaments; and one should deliver sentient beings according to how they ought to be delivered.

That is to say, by means of the practice of non-practice, one manifests various forms and appearances; having attained purity of body, one manifests freedom from delusion so that sentient beings may know it.
That is to say, by means of the existence of non-existence, they emit all manner of pure and wondrous sounds, enabling the multitude to clearly understand various different languages.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
This constitutes tenfold purity, and that bodhisattva is likewise fully endowed with these ten points.
What are the ten points through which sentient beings are guided to perceive the Buddha-activity? They are:
causing sentient beings who abide therein to attain faith and orientation toward all Buddhas.
That is to say, establishing sentient beings through the sounds of the Buddha-dharma;
that is to say, delivering sentient beings so that they may be born in buddha-fields;
that is to say, providing relief and security for sentient beings so that they may place their faith in all Buddhas.
That is to say: to guide and benefit sentient beings by hearing the sound of the Buddha-dharma;
to deliver and rescue sentient beings by manifesting the Buddha’s spiritual transformations;
and to bring peace to sentient beings by contemplating their conduct according to what is appropriate, thereby perfecting the single mind.
That is to say: to bring peace and accord to sentient beings and to adorn all Buddhas;
that is to say, to give rise to the bodhicitta by means of benefiting and bringing peace to sentient beings;
and that is to say, to eternally bring peace to sentient beings by fully perfecting the Buddha-wisdom.
"By this, noble son!
Through these ten matters, that bodhisattva brings peace and benefit to sentient beings.
Having thus brought peace to sentient beings by fulfilling the ten perfections, that bodhisattva universally performs the ten deeds of a Buddha for the sake of all sentient beings."
What are the ten?
First, it means that those bodhisattvas perform buddha-work by means of vocal sound in order to deliver the assembled congregations.
Second, it means that upon seeing those bodhisattvas, one performs buddha-work in order to guide sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
Third, it means that as soon as those bodhisattvas move, they perform the Buddha-work because their mental application is pure.
Fourth, it means that those bodhisattvas shake all lands while performing the Buddha-work, thereby simultaneously turning back the three evil realms.
Fifth, it means that those bodhisattvas manifest their births in various locations to perform the deeds of a Buddha, for the purpose of correctly gladdening the minds of sentient beings.
Sixth, it means that those bodhisattvas perform the deeds of a Buddha through all appropriate conduct, guiding and benefiting sentient beings so that their minds are free from delusion.
Seventh, it means that those bodhisattvas perform buddha-activities while ascending through radiance, for they uphold and deliver countless sentient beings.
Eighth, it means that those bodhisattvas perform buddha-activities while manifesting the cultivation of various virtues, for they exhort and establish sentient beings in countless virtues.

Ninth, it means that when those bodhisattvas attain the realization of equal enlightenment and perform the deeds of a Buddha, they cause all sentient beings to understand that all phenomena are like illusions.

Tenth, it means that those bodhisattvas turn the wheel of Dharma and perform the buddha-work, preaching the Dharma for the sake of the entire world so that the jewels of the noble ones may long endure.
"O son of good family!

That bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the ten deeds of a Buddha in order to deliver countless people, to rescue countless sentient beings, to fulfill immeasurable vows, to establish the mental conduct of all beings, and to eternally establish the work of a Buddha."
10. Chapter on the Manifestation of the External Body, etc., from the *Bodhisattva Sūtra*: Chapter Ten, "The Manifestation of the External Body. "Furthermore, son of good family!

There is a samādhi of right reception for bodhisattva mahāsattvas called 'the indestructibility of the body. By means of this, the bodhisattva abides in this mental state such that the body remains indestructible, and they attain fulfillment in the ten kinds of wishlessness."
What are the ten?
First, having no expectations regarding any lands.
Second, having no expectations regarding any directions.
Third, to have no expectations regarding any conceptualizations;
fourth, to have no expectations regarding any sentient beings;
fifth, to have no expectations regarding any phenomena.
Sixth, there is no expectation regarding the practices of all bodhisattvas.
Seventh, there is no expectation regarding the vows of all bodhisattvas.
Eighth, there is no expectation regarding meditative concentrations.
Ninth, to have no expectations regarding all forms.
Tenth, to likewise have no expectations regarding the stages of practice.
These are the ten.
When a bodhisattva attains the ten kinds of hopelessness, they are able to abide in the samādhi of the indestructible conduct of all bodies.
How does a bodhisattva attain the samādhi of the indestructible body of sentient beings?
O son of noble family!
A bodhisattva enters meditative absorption within his own body and awakens to the external body; he enters meditative absorption within the external body and awakens to his own body.
He enters meditative absorption with a single body and awakens with many bodies; he enters meditative absorption with many bodies and awakens with a single body.
Entering meditative absorption with a human body and awakening with the body of a ghost or spirit;
entering meditative absorption with the body of a ghost or spirit and awakening with the body of a dragon;
entering meditative absorption with the body of a dragon and awakening with the body of a *chiliang* (subtle) spirit.
One may enter meditative absorption with the substantial and sincere spirit-body and awaken with the celestial body;
or one may enter meditative absorption with the celestial body and awaken with the Brahma-body;
or one may enter meditative absorption with the Brahma-body and awaken within the desire realm.
Some may enter meditative absorption in the desire realm and awaken in the form realm;
some may enter meditative absorption in the form realm and awaken in the formless realm;
or some may enter meditative absorption in the formless realm and manifest in the hells to awaken there.
Sometimes they enter meditative absorption within the hells and awaken while manifesting as hungry ghosts;
sometimes they enter meditative absorption among hungry ghosts and awaken while manifesting as animals;
or they enter meditative absorption in stillness and awaken amidst the multitude.
Or they may enter meditative absorption within a thousand bodies and awaken in a bodiless state;
or they may enter meditative absorption within a body and awaken in a state of countless bodies;
or they may enter meditative absorption within countless billions of nayutas of bodies and manifest as empty bodies upon awakening.
Or they may enter meditative absorption in Jambudvīpa and awaken in Godānīya;
or enter absorption in Godānīya and awaken in Uttarakuru;
or enter absorption in Uttarakuru and awaken in Pūrvavideha.
Some enter meditative absorption in Pūrvavideha and awaken throughout the three continents;
some enter meditative absorption in the three continents and awaken throughout the four continents;
some enter meditative absorption in the four continents and awaken throughout the sentient beings of all three realms.
They enter meditative absorption throughout the entire realm of the ocean and awaken within that same oceanic realm for the sake of sentient beings.
Or they enter meditative absorption upon Mount Sumeru and awaken on the mountain’s base; or they enter meditative absorption on the mountain’s base and awaken upon the mountain.
Or they enter meditative absorption amidst the mountains of the seven jewels and awaken upon those mountains as well.
He may enter meditative absorption amidst various kinds [of forms] and likewise awaken amidst various diverse types;
he may enter meditative absorption amidst pure arrays of various flowers, incenses, and many jewels, and likewise manifest awakening amidst pure arrays of various fragrant flowers and many jewels.
Throughout the entire realm of the four continents, they enter into meditative absorption in accordance with the mental inclinations of all sentient beings;
furthermore, they manifest within the realm of the four continents, bringing all sentient beings to awakening according to their mental inclinations.
Within a thousand lands, he enters meditative absorption throughout their entire extent, and likewise manifests awakening within a thousand lands.
Within a trichiliocosm, he enters meditative absorption throughout its entire extent, and likewise manifests awakening within a trichiliocosm.

He enters meditative absorption within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields, and likewise manifests awakening within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddha-fields.
He enters meditative absorption within incalculable buddha-fields, and likewise manifests awakening within incalculable buddha-fields.
He enters meditative absorption in incalculable buddha-fields and likewise manifests awakening in incalculable buddha-fields.
He enters meditative absorption in immeasurable and infinite buddha-fields; in short, he manifests awakening throughout all such fields.
From a single world-system as numerous as motes of dust, they proceed to four world-systems;
then to a thousand world-systems;
and further to a trichiliocosm of three thousand great thousand world-systems.
Again, they reach billions of nayutas of lands;
again, they reach asaṃkhyeya lands, even unto the infinite and the incalculable;
having passed beyond these infinite and incalculable lands, they enter into meditative absorption throughout such numbers and likewise awaken within them.
Entering meditative absorption within a single atom, he again manifests awakening within as many atoms as there are in such superior buddha-fields.
Emerging from meditative absorption within as many atoms as there are in such superior buddha-fields, he again manifests awakening within a single atom.
Entering into meditative absorption within a single śrāvaka, he again manifests as countless śrāvakas and brings them to awakening.
Entering into meditative absorption within a single pratyekabuddha, he again manifests as countless pratyekabuddhas and brings them to awakening.
Entering meditative absorption within one's own body, one again manifests awakening within the bodies of countless Buddhas;
entering meditative absorption within the bodies of countless Buddhas, one again manifests awakening within one's own body.
Entering meditative absorption within the span of a single thought-moment, they manifest awakening throughout billions of eons;
entering meditative absorption throughout billions of eons, they manifest awakening in the time it takes for a thought to arise.
At times one awakens, and at times one enters meditative absorption;
or one may enter absorption and awaken simultaneously;
or one may enter absorption while focused on a prior accumulation [of merit] and awaken while manifesting a subsequent accumulation.
Some enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) through the accumulation of the future and attain awakening through the accumulation of the present;
others enter meditative absorption through the accumulation of the present and likewise attain awakening through the accumulation of the present.
One enters meditative absorption through the accumulation of the fundamental and awakens regarding the three periods of time;
one awakens through the accumulation of time;
one enters meditative absorption through the accumulation of time, enters meditative absorption regarding the three periods of time, and awakens regarding the original non-existence.
Or, while experiencing meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within the original non-existence, one suddenly awakens back to that original non-existence.
"For example, son of good family!
When a person is afflicted by a spirit, having already been seized by the spirit, it takes control and moves him about; he no longer possesses autonomy, but follows only that spirit!"
This would mean that he follows after another's body, and his own body would no longer attain mastery.
It is the same for the Bodhisattva!
Having attained this samādhi, he may enter meditative absorption internally while remaining awake externally.
Externally one enters meditative absorption, while internally one remains awakened.
It is like a dead man whose corpse is employed by another spirit; though he is pursued in his tasks and turned about in all directions, it is merely a transformation!
That which employs them is the supernatural power of another.
Thus, noble son!
Having attained this concentration, the bodhisattva enters into meditative absorption; through discernment he enters into meditative absorption, and through discernment he further awakens.
They enter meditative absorption through impartial discernment and awaken through impartial discernment.
Just as the mind is sovereign, so too are the transformations of Māra free and unrestrained:
he may manifest as one or as many, and he may manifest as many or as one.
They do not perish as a single body and yet manifest as many; nor do they perish as many bodies and yet transform into a single body.
At that time, even that single body does not possess the nature of a single body; they do not manifest multiplicity by knowing oneness, nor do they know oneness by manifesting multiplicity.
Whether one or many, they arise from the One alone!
It is the same for the Bodhisattva:
while entering meditative absorption within a single body, they awaken within many bodies.
Or, one may enter meditative absorption with many bodies and awaken with a single body.
It is like a single expanse of earth, which is of a single flavor.

Within that single expanse of earth, the various villages and towns plant different seeds, resulting in different flavors; yet the earth itself does not conceive of this, nor do those flavors possess any manifold consciousness.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Having attained this concentration of mind, he enters meditative absorption as one and awakens to many; within many meditative absorptions, he awakens as one.
O son of good family!
This is called the eighth bodhisattva-samādhi of the bodhisattva mahāsattva, known as "Discriminating All Bodies."
"When that bodhisattva attains his dwelling place, ten kinds of renown reach him, and his fame flows forth constantly.
What are these ten?
First, he is praised by the Tathāgata."
Second, they attain the majestic power of equality of the Tathāgata.
Third, it means that as a Buddha, they clearly understand all dharmas without any obstruction.
Fourth, it means that they are the most honored, for they receive the offerings of all the world’s extremities.
Fifth, it is called "universal knowledge," because it clearly understands all phenomena.
Sixth, it is called "the guide," because it serves as the ultimate reliance for all in the world.
Seventh, it means being a guide, for the purpose of clearly understanding and entering into all phenomena.
Eighth, it means being the unsurpassed teacher, the fundamental source of the dharmas for sentient beings, because universal wisdom is without limit.
Ninth, it is for the sake of raising up illumination, by employing wisdom in accordance with all supreme worldly great illuminations.
Tenth, it is for the sake of the ten powers, to attain the most auspicious state through all performed actions;
it is to discern all phenomena, reaching them through mindfulness by means of that wisdom.
Possessing the practice of non-attachment, he is said to manifest universally within the True Dharma Wheel and has attained mastery.
By means of these ten dharmas of renown, the bodhisattva thereby possesses the highest fame.
“Furthermore, there are ten kinds of illumination possessed by Bodhisattvas that are exceedingly majestic and radiant.
What are these ten?
The first is that their illumination is equal to that of all Buddhas.”

Second, it means that regarding the ultimate world, one gives rise to the radiance of wisdom through the clear exposition of the fundamental Dharma, thereby illuminating and manifesting all phenomena.
Third, regarding all sentient beings, one employs luminous illumination to provide various clear expositions.
Fourth, by means of countless luminosities, they advance and guide with the luminosity of the field of Dharma.
Fifth, by means of the luminosity of the Dharma-realm, they cause it to arise, manifest, and be proclaimed.
Sixth, by moving all phenomena, yet not destroying their clarity.
Seventh, because all phenomena are without desire and so forth, and because they are without activity, one does not destroy clarity.
Eighth, because sentient beings are without desire and so forth, they contemplate all that moves in the world without obstruction.
Ninth, because they clearly and brilliantly illuminate that which is established by all Buddhas without interruption.
Tenth is the boundless realm of all Buddhas; because all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, their clarity is supreme, as nothing in the world can be destroyed.
By means of these ten clarities, the Bodhisattva attains radiant brilliance.
“Furthermore, there are ten matters by which a bodhisattva attains clear understanding through the teaching on the state of non-attachment.
What are these ten?
First, skillfully cultivating pliancy in bodily conduct.”
Second, the absence of harsh speech;
third, a supple and gentle nature;
fourth, dwelling nowhere.
Fifth, it means that the mind is without fabrication.
Sixth, it means that conduct is without purposeful action.
Seventh, it means that there is no disparagement of the Dharma.
Eighth, wisdom has nothing from which it arises.
Ninth, there is no conceptualization regarding phenomena.
Tenth, one accords with those [phenomena] through wisdom.
This is called the samādhi of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva for subduing Māra.
By means of manifold practices he subdues it; by means of the one he makes it many, attaining realization through correct meditative absorption.
He practices the practice of non-practice, yet practices within practice.
One esteems oneself as great, equaling the Buddha;
yet one treats the small as vast and secure,
and the expansive and open as narrow and petty.
That which is approached has no destination, and that which is reached has no point of departure.
Taking formlessness as the body, one is without body within the state of having a body.
One enters right meditative absorption through awakening.
One awakens through right reception;
there is seeing within non-seeing, and non-seeing within seeing.
This is called the tenth.
"Furthermore, there are ten matters that constitute transformation.
What are these ten?
First, all realms of transformation are entirely states of meditative concentration."

For example, it is like a great mantra whose words and practices are universally proclaimed, manifesting various forms and clearly establishing that which is beyond reproach. What is manifested is a metaphor that transcends the words of the mantra, yet it accords with illusion; thus, one vigorously establishes wisdom and understands the proper timing.
Regarding illusions, they manifest names, practice and learn their arts, and through wisdom attain thorough penetration.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!

By means of equanimous meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), they manifest awakening through the peerless; by means of the peerless, they enter meditative absorption; and by means of equanimity, they awaken.
It is, for example, like when the devas and asuras fought together, and the devas were victorious while the asuras were defeated.
Śakra-devendra, with his body seven hundred yojanas in height, surrounded himself with the fourfold army.
The asura then further transformed his body to a height of hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, such that all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven beheld him; his retinue was majestic and orderly.
Furthermore, the asura was profoundly learned and possessed clear understanding.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this!
He is fully proficient in the illusory practice of wisdom, yet that wisdom is inexhaustible.
Such a Bodhisattva is truly a Bodhisattva indeed!
That Bodhisattva Prajñāmāyā enters meditative absorption through non-interruption and awakens within interruption.

It is like a great mantra called "Delusive Charm": by means of this incantation, one takes various seeds, scatters them upon the ground, and immediately obtains their stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits to eat.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Having attained single-minded concentration, they are able to manifest various forms and bring them to awakening.
It is, for example, like when men and women have been in union for a long time, resulting in conception; once the embryo is formed and the ten months are fulfilled, a complete being is born.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!

They nurture the womb of universal wisdom, fully perfecting all vows; through their vast inner nature, they attain the light of wisdom and abide in indestructible concentration, universally awakening to all realms of existence.
They experience meditative absorption within the various realms of existence, yet awaken within the indestructible concentration.
It is like the palaces of the nāgas, which depend upon the earth yet also appear in the sky;
they do not, however, move the sky.
Nor does he cause alarm among the nāgas.
In space there are also gandharvas, and there are also nāgas;
yet that space neither increases nor decreases.
Or, desiring shade while it is sunny, they remain motionless in the midst of space;
yet their palaces continue to rest either upon the earth or in the void.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!

By attaining this illusion-like samādhi, one enters meditative absorption regarding that which has signs, and awakens to that which is signless; one enters meditative absorption regarding that which is signless, and awakens to that which is signless.
"It is like the palace of Brahmā, named the Pure Treasury Sustaining the World, the palace where the supreme Brahmā dwells;
it may manifest as a thousand worlds,
or it may manifest as ten thousand worlds."
Sometimes he manifests a hundred thousand worlds; sometimes he manifests a trichiliocosm.
He manifests among the palaces of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and ghosts, as well as among the world of human beings.

In some places he manifests as Mount Sumeru, and among the mountains of the seven treasures, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Black Jewel Mountains, and the Snowy Mountains; throughout the four continents, the provinces, kingdoms, counties, towns, and villages; among kings and the human realm; and reaching even to the abodes of Brahmā—there is nowhere he does not pervade.
Just as a bright mirror reflects one's facial features,
so it is with the Bodhisattva!
Abiding in this samādhi, there is no wisdom among all things that is not clearly penetrating.
There is nowhere it does not enter, yet it is entirely equal; it reaches everywhere, its wisdom-illumination penetrating and clear.
That Bodhisattva is also like this!
By means of this light of mastery over all bodies, meditative concentrations, and buddha-fields, he perceives the entire lineage of Buddhas and transforms all various kinds of beings.
Transcending the seeds of phenomena, they fulfill the seeds of the practice of liberation;
likewise, through the seed of meditative concentration, they stir and give rise to the seed of awakening, universally manifesting to attain the seed of wisdom, and abiding in the seed of knowledge.
“The Bodhisattva attains the Perfection of Liberation through ten kinds of manifestations.
What are these ten?
First is the manifestation of attaining Buddhahood, which is like empty space.”
Second, exhausting the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*).
Third, through the inspiration of a bodhisattva, reaching the state of non-destruction, attaining mastery over destruction, and thus achieving the perfection of liberation (*pāramitā*).
Fourth, the practice of the bodhisattva moves great vows.
Fifth, the practice enters the conduct of the Tathāgata, the perfection of buddha-activities.
Sixth, one moves all lands, manifesting every kind of practice for solitary dwelling.
Seventh, they cause all lands to tremble, relying upon manifest clarity.
Eighth, they move all sentient beings through inconceivable conduct, fully comprehending profound matters and moving them through wisdom.
Ninth, to move and distinguish various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
Tenth, by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajrasamādhi*) and the profound transformative meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), to awaken through wisdom.
By these ten practices of concentration, the bodhisattva fulfills all varieties [of qualities].
"Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva can manifest as a Buddha, abide as one who is like a Buddha, and transform the Wheel of Dharma. He establishes emanations and universally manifests the radiance of a Tathāgata. He delivers those whose wills are set upon the Mahāyāna; he subdues them therein, exalting their minds, and through the power of his spiritual footprints (ṛddhipāda), he moves them with infinite transcendence, becoming most honored among bodhisattvas."

The Bodhisattva of Clear Comprehension possesses the samādhi of unattached wisdom; through the attainment of non-attainment, he moves others by means of hundreds of thousands of millions of Dharma-gates and turns the wheel of the Dharma.

The Bodhisattva is free from all hindrances and clearly understands all conditioned activities; being fully aware that they are devoid of conceptual thought, he is able to comprehend them all at once through his luminous wisdom, manifesting a transformative influence throughout the three periods of time without any obstruction.
By means of these ten matters, one is greatly moved; this is the practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, leading to the attainment of the *pāramitās*.
O son of noble family!

It is through the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discernment of bodily conduct that they reach that upon which they may rely and abide—the wisdom of great virtue, skillful means, and definitive realization.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, Scroll Two;
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.

Chapter Eleven: The Analysis of Bodily Activity and the Great Wisdom on Emptiness Furthermore, son of good family, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva regards his own body, he exhaustively realizes that the body and all its parts are like an illusion; whatever is seen by the eye accords with the dharma-realm.

The arising of the bodhisattva’s concentration is also equal to his body; from each and every pore of his hair, he manifests all dharma-realms, and the bodhisattva abides therein in right meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He too dwells merely in the nature of illusion!
Furthermore, all the lands that are known are likewise like the nature of those phenomena.
By knowing all phenomena, one then knows billions of nayutas of incalculable lands, and further knows the attainment of non-attainment.

In lands as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, throughout all those lands, there are Buddhas currently present, surrounded by Bodhisattvas; they are all perfectly pure and utterly refined, all courageous, adorned with noble conduct and eloquence, embellished with immeasurable awakening, radiant like the sun, and beautifully arrayed with various jewels.

Whether for ten eons, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or a billion, or a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas, or for that which is incalculable, limitless, boundless, and infinite—an exhaustive number that reaches even to the number of eons as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field—one practices the various bodhisattva deeds; the basis upon which one dwells therein can never be exhausted.
“The Bodhisattva enters meditative absorption in that state and yet awakens from it; he enters meditative absorption here and awakens from that concentration.
He universally enters all lands, transforming the multitudes and the realms of sentient beings therein, causing them all to enter the Dharma-realm, and clearly comprehending all wisdoms of the past.”

Furthermore, he manifests in various places to preach the sūtras and the Dharma; he is clearly enlightened and possesses no attachments, his unobstructed eye discerns all things, and he attains mastery over the dharmas, transcending them with ease;
his ear’s discernment brings him to the perfection of transcendence (pāramitā);
and his nose’s discernment likewise employs skillful means (upāya).
That which is discriminated by the mouth is fully understood;
that which is discriminated by the body is likewise thoroughly comprehended;
and that which is discriminated by the mind is fully endowed with wisdom and mindfulness.
By means of this wisdom, he attains such clarity and thereby acquires ten billion *koṭis* of *dhāraṇīs*.
What are these ten? They are:
through the Dharma, universally conforming to all lands.
One accomplishes ten billion times ten thousand pure practices;
understands ten billion times ten thousand divine harmonies, and enters the practice of universal wisdom.
One attains the full perfection of ten billion times ten thousand supernormal powers.
He attains entry into ten billion times ten thousand concentrations and mental activities;
he attains ten billion times ten thousand supernormal powers, bringing them to full completion;
and he attains the increase of ten billion times ten thousand powers.
One attains ten billion times ten thousand qualities of sincerity;
one attains the manifestation of ten billion times ten thousand abodes;
and one attains ten billion times ten thousand stirrings.
These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are ten essences of the bodhisattva through which they achieve hundreds of thousands of millions.
There are ten spheres of practice for the bodhisattva, fully perfected to the extent of hundreds of thousands of millions.
Bodhisattvas have ten treasuries, which transcend billions of equalities.
Bodhisattvas have ten practices, which manifest radiant brilliance throughout billions.
Bodhisattvas have ten stages, by which they proclaim billions of teachings.
The Bodhisattva has ten vows that surpass billions of virtuous practices;
the Bodhisattva has ten sincere repentances that establish billions of cultivated virtues.
Bodhisattvas have ten illuminations, through which they attain billions of pure practices.
Bodhisattvas have ten superior orientations, through which they bring billions of qualities to self-manifestation.
The Bodhisattva has ten expositions, by which they attain the virtue of a billion illuminations.
The Bodhisattva has ten fruits of purity, through which they reach a billion states and achieve purification.
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s practice of possessing countless bodies;
accomplishing countless virtues;
and fulfilling the virtue of selflessness.
Accomplishing countless practices;
cultivating inconceivable virtues;
performing virtues beyond measure.
Fulfilling the practice of non-self;
bringing about the attainment of what is not virtuous;
possessing inexhaustible mindfulness of the virtue of non-self.
By means of these practices, the bodhisattva fulfills all virtues, attains the practice of equanimity, and thereby adorns themselves;
they attain manifest joy, harmony, and gentleness;
they attain the upholding of the teachings and the performance of offerings, thereby becoming exceptionally exalted.
Those who attain the incomparable become courageous;
regarding this Dharma, the Bodhisattva attains mastery.

"Relying on this samādhi, the bodhisattva establishes himself before the Tathāgatas in ten buddha-fields to the east, as numerous as the atoms of countless thousands of worlds, using each and every name; for each and every name, those [Tathāgatas] in the ten buddha-fields are as many as the atoms [of those fields], such that no one is able to conceive of their limit."
From that single atom, one divides it into countless thousands of Buddha-fields, as numerous as atoms, pervading them all; yet there is no perception of this, nor is there any increase or decrease.
Just as there is no increase or decrease in the single non-awakening, so it is throughout all lands as numerous as atoms.
As it is for that which is done in the east, so it is in the south, west, north, the intermediate directions, above, and below!
The number of points where attachment can occur, even when a single atom is divided, is also as stated above.
That Bodhisattva is able to establish them and can universally manifest his body therein.
This Bodhisattva is able to universally purify all that is established within the various Buddha-fields.
Because the body of the Tathāgata is limitless, he attains mastery over light;
furthermore, because it is inconceivable, he is able to produce transformations, causing [the light] to appear everywhere!
"What the Tathāgata’s ears proclaim is likewise immeasurable;
what the Tathāgata’s nose discerns is also limitless;
and what the Tathāgata’s mouth discerns manifests as equality."
The Tathāgata’s body moves in accordance with what is subtle and smooth;
the manifestations of the Tathāgata’s mind are beyond limit.
The knowledge and mindfulness of the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment are likewise immeasurable.
They proclaim the pure voice of the Tathāgata;
they universally manifest the Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata without ever turning back;
and they cause all beings to universally know the holy assembly of the Tathāgata as being infinite in number.
The Tathāgata awakens to the Dharma and is likewise limitless, universally guiding and leading.
He universally manifests and brings forth the root of the Tathāgata’s merits;
he manifests entry into the Tathāgata’s meditative absorptions and the Tathāgata’s virtues.
Practicing throughout the three periods of time, countless Tathāgatas appear and manifest all dharmas,
establishing them and proclaiming them through their voices.
This is the tenth.
"Manifestly establishing the land of the Tathāgata,
he universally rains down all dharmas with the Buddha’s voice,
causing that voice to be heard throughout all lands."
He extensively proclaims the Buddha’s right concentration (*samāpatti*),
and likewise universally proclaims all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of worthy sages (*ārya*).
He establishes the inconceivable Dharma of all Buddhas.
All dharmas that are proclaimed are entirely like illusions and transformations.
One expounds all dharmas without any attachment,
clearly illuminating the entire field of all dharmas.
They universally and fully manifest the practices of all the virtues of the Tathāgatas;
this is the tenth.
All meditative concentrations accord with and lead toward the illusory nature of phenomena; they establish the mind as being like an illusion, understanding it to be without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva attains complete mastery over this Dharma-realm; it is precisely for this reason that they are established as Bodhisattvas!

"Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, through each and every name among the various mentalities, manifest countless Buddha-lands and Tathāgatas as numerous as the dust motes of thousands of worlds!"
Each individual name is as numerous as atoms;
for each atom, ten Buddha-fields are established, continuing until nine times the number of atoms of Buddha-fields have been established, yet there is neither increase nor decrease.
That there is no one who can know that which is grasped and clung to—this is what is established by the bodhisattva.
Cultivating practices that correspond to non-attainment and are beyond measure is likewise established by the mind.
It is established by the mind of non-attachment;
it is established by mindfulness because there is no delusion regarding all phenomena;
it is established by conduct because of the discernment of wisdom regarding all phenomena.
Because all dharmas are the locus of what is received, they are established through practice;
because one accords with and reveres all dharmas, one is also established through awakening to the Path;
and because one practices and universally proclaims the Dharma, one also establishes countless sentient beings.
By means of establishing supernormal powers through discernment, one practices without arising because of the application of skillful means and wisdom regarding phenomena.
Because that which is established is clearly understood and because the dharma-realm is without attachment, one likewise abides in the practice of wisdom through cultivation and entry.
Because their infinite wisdom is purified, they also abide in perfect enlightenment;
because they manifest spiritual transformations throughout all lands,
the Bodhisattva abides in these meditative concentrations and thereby attains the gates of the ten oceans.
What are the ten? First, it is called the manifestation of the ocean of Buddhas, because it guides all oceans accordingly.
Second, it is called the transcendence of the ocean of dharmas, because one has completed the practice of the ocean of wisdom.
Third, they abide in all luminous splendors because they have no attachments regarding sentient beings.
Fourth, they move others through wisdom because they employ the spreading of sounds.
Fifth, they contemplate the ocean of all sentient beings because they accord with skillful means and wisdom.
Sixth, they thoroughly understand the ocean of the mind, for they know the countless minds without any dualistic observation.
Seventh, they fulfill the ocean of practice, because they are fully endowed with their vows.
Eighth, because they are fully endowed with the ocean of all vows and practices, they lack even a single ninth dharma.
Tenth, because they bring all beings to the path of awakening.
These are the ten.
The Bodhisattva brings to fulfillment the ocean of all virtues and dharmas.
There are ten matters by which a Bodhisattva attains supreme honor.
What are these ten?
First, by means of being a supreme honor, one guides all beings in accordance with the truth.
Second, by seeking the most sublime state, one transforms and guides sentient beings.
Third, by seeking the upward-aspiring honor, one then attains all pure conducts (*brahmacarya*).
Fourth, to attain supreme power and seek to fully acquire it.
Fifth, to seek peerlessness among all that is most extreme in the world.
Sixth, to seek unsurpassability because of surpassing Māra.
Seventh, he seeks clarity and lucidity in order to deliver all beings from the evil realms.
Eighth, he seeks non-reliance regarding all places of birth.
Ninth, he seeks to be preeminent among all the Buddha-dharmas.
Tenth, seeking to attain sovereignty over all sentient beings and possessing courageous vigor—
these are the ten supreme and honorable dharmas of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, there are ten matters by which a bodhisattva brings forth [benefit] within the realm of sentient beings.
What are these ten?
First, they constantly resolve to leave the household life in order to deliver sentient beings.
Second, they are without regression, advancing with the most fierce vigor.
Third, seeking reliance upon all Buddhas in order to receive and practice their teachings.
Fourth, possessing infinite power to advance in all dharmas.
Fifth, the power of tranquil concentration, which brings mastery over all dharmas.
Sixth, the mind is without regression, due to the power of compliant guidance.
Seventh, there is mastery over meaning, due to the fundamental power of the Dharma.
Eighth, one acts as great wisdom, due to the power of proclaiming the Dharma without obstruction.
Ninth is the power of valor, because it is established by the Dharma.
Tenth is the power of discernment, because it proclaims immeasurable wisdom.
These are called the ten kinds of powers.
"Furthermore, they attain ten kinds of great heroic strength.
What are the ten?
First is the strength of supreme vigor."
Second, the power that cannot be surpassed;
third, immeasurable power;
fourth, the power of excellent cultivation.
Fifth, the power of immovability;
sixth, the power of non-arising;
seventh, the power of non-anger.
Eighth, the power of constant wisdom.
Ninth, the power of diligent establishment.
Tenth, the power of expansive compassion.
These are the ten powers.
Furthermore, there are another ten powers.
What are these ten?
First, the power of cultivating disciplined conduct;
second, the power of the purity of wisdom;
third, the power of the purity that transcends phenomena.
Fourth is the power of the Dharma-body;
fifth is the power of the lands of all dharmas;
sixth is the power of the radiance of the Dharma-light.
Seventh, the power of the disposition toward the Dharma.
Eighth, the power of indestructibility.
Ninth, the power of cultivating virtuous conduct.
Tenth is the power of cultivating diligence.
These are the ten powers.
Furthermore, there are ten other powers.
What are the ten?
First, the power of a great man (mahāpuruṣa).
Second, the power of a true hero (samyak-vīra).
Third, the power established by the Perfectly Enlightened One;
fourth, the power of the roots of virtue cultivated in previous lives;
fifth, the power of immeasurable roots of virtue applied according to what is appropriate.
Sixth, the power of the Tathāgata;
seventh, the power of universal engagement;
eighth, the power of equality regarding the three periods of time.
Ninth, they attain the power of the bodhisattva’s earth-like conduct.
Tenth, they attain the power of the bodhisattva’s pure conduct of faith and inclination.
These are the ten powers.
"Furthermore, there are ten powers.
What are these ten powers?
First, the bodhisattva’s power of detachment from transmigration."
Second, the power of the bodhisattva’s conformity with conditions;
third, the power of the bodhisattva’s mastery over their own nature;
fourth, the power of the bodhisattva’s cultivation of inner purity of nature.
Fifth, the bodhisattva cultivates the roots of all virtues through the power of various practices.
Sixth, the bodhisattva’s practice of the Dharma is the supreme power.
Seventh, the body possesses the power of non-attachment.
Eighth, the power by which a bodhisattva achieves completion;
ninth, the power of a bodhisattva’s entry into skillful means and wisdom;
tenth, the power of a bodhisattva’s faith and inclination toward the fundamental purity of all phenomena.
These are the ten.
Furthermore, there are ten powers.
What are the ten?
First, because of the power of abiding in the universal world in tranquil seclusion;
second, because of the power of being peerless among all beings;
third, because of the power of being unequaled throughout all things.
Fourth, by means of the power to transform sentient beings through all virtuous conduct;
fifth, by means of the power of being unshakable while remaining within birth and death;
sixth, by means of the power of crossing over all birth and death, pure as a lotus flower.
Seventh, universally manifesting all guides in order to subdue the powers of Māra;
eighth, appearing to comply with the factions of Māra in order to achieve the power of the Mahāyāna;
ninth, transforming those within the three realms through the power of non-abiding.
Tenth is the power of universally exhorting and advancing those in the ten directions because of being free from all obstructions. These are the ten.
By means of these countless dharmas, the bodhisattva accomplishes his virtuous transformation of others.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva gives rise to practices that fulfill all vows; he illuminates them, makes them manifest, universally responds by appearing in various forms, and brings them all to completion.
Thus he attains vast and great progress in wisdom, increasing it and making it extensively pure.
These are the ten concentrations conducive to purity.
Those manifold virtues are boundless, and his wisdom is likewise unimpeded.
His bodhisattva practice is also without limit.
The vehicle of that bodhisattva’s virtues is immeasurable and difficult to extol.
Furthermore, the sphere of activity of that bodhisattva is difficult to delimit, and that which the bodhisattva enters cannot be fathomed.
The transformations manifested by that bodhisattva are likewise boundless;
the purity of that bodhisattva is likewise inconceivable;
and the practices cultivated by that bodhisattva are likewise impossible to exhaust.
Furthermore, the noble and holy Dharma of these Bodhisattvas is likewise unsurpassed.
Because it cannot be apprehended, there is no limit to its contemplation.

That which can be attained by these Bodhisattvas, that which serves as the cause for their arising, that which all Bodhisattvas should practice, and that which all Bodhisattvas ought to realize—[all this is unsurpassed].
Furthermore, that bodhisattva’s clarity reaches wherever he goes.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva can see through to the very end.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva’s luminous wisdom passes beyond all things.
Furthermore, this is that which can be known and seen through the Dharma-practice of the Bodhisattva.
Moreover, it is that which the Bodhisattva’s practice ought to attain.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva attains mastery over all places of wisdom regarding the practice of all dharmas.
These are the ten.
One who abides in this great samādhi attains that which is innumerable, limitless, immeasurable, boundless, inexhaustible, beyond measure, inconceivable, and free from the notion of self-attainment.
These are the ten.
By means of these meditative attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*), the bodhisattva enters into each and every practice;
whether in concentration or in awakening, they fully comprehend all practices of meditative absorption.
He clearly understands countless concentrations and fully comprehends all complete concentrations; he also knows the increase and decrease of concentration.
Furthermore, he understands that concentrations are like illusions and clearly perceives the activities seen within concentration;
he also knows the causal origins of concentration.
He also knows the boundaries of concentration;
he is clearly enlightened regarding the tranquility of concentration;
and he also knows the stillness of concentration.
He also knows the practice of meditative mindfulness.

"For example, from the palace of the Anavatapta Dragon King’s lake, four great rivers flow forth; they overflow, clear and transparent, stainless, unclouded, and unsullied, pure and flawless, sweet, fragrant, and clean."
Surrounding it on four sides are four eyes and mouths from which [the waters] flow forth:
one eye is named Vaṃśa;
the second eye is named Vakṣu.
The one with three eyes is named Śemuṇḍa;
the one with four eyes is named Nitya.
Their confluence flows northward, while the Vakṣu flows southward.
That serpent flows to the east, while the Ganges flows to the west;
each winds and turns in circles, and likewise in all four directions, filling and pervading them entirely.
Furthermore, that great river encircles [the mountain] seven times.

Between these rivers, there are blue lotuses, red lotuses, white lotuses, and yellow lotuses; with the radiant colors of the various celestial jewels, they are brilliant, wondrous, and pure, illuminating one another, appearing fresh and clean, forever free from defilement, and clearly visible, shining with penetrating clarity.
Each leaf is distinct and clearly manifested, such that no painter could ever depict it.
Its supple and vibrant colors shine forth, and its sounds are profoundly exquisite;
the colors of its sublime wisdom are beyond the limits of artistic representation, and its countless celestial phrases and texts bring universal joy.
The various leaves overlap one another, their colors exquisitely beautiful; they are fragrant, lovely, and of extraordinary beauty, their radiance shining forth.
Adorned with countless varieties of diverse jewels, their manifold colors are as infinite as the light of the Sun God emerging from his palace, penetrating and illuminating everything.
“Those various flowers, radiant and brilliant, shine upon one another with such splendor that they can eclipse the essential light of the sun.
Those various blossoms float along the current of the river.”
There are devas who, as the river swirls, turns, floats, and sinks, wander amidst various flowers.
These flowers, rising and falling, bowing and lifting, possess wondrous colors that blaze brilliantly, shining with the distinct luster of jewels.

As the sunlight shines down in its curved brilliance, the dark and the yellow are brought to rest; the radiance of the sun is like the movement of various flowers, and the sounds flowing from the rivers surpass even the music of the heavens.
“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this!
He possesses four kinds of eloquence that flow forth, filling the ocean of universal wisdom.
It is like the great river of fragrance, which has the wondrous color of silver and flows from the mouth of a horse.”
Its bottom is entirely covered with silver sand.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
With pure wisdom, he accords with all modes of conduct, and from his mouth issues forth meanings that accord with and follow [the truth].

The practices of all Tathāgatas, the practices of all meanings, the Dharma of skillful giving, the wisdom-light of all dharmas, and the unimpeded wisdom that thoroughly discerns and understands—these lead one back to the ocean of knowledge;
like the great river of harmony, they possess the color of vajra, flowing forth from the mouth of the lion, with its sands also the color of vajra.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
He emits the radiant light of the Dharma, possessing the golden-vajra color of a Buddha, delighting therein while illuminating the entire world.
Delighting oneself with adamantine wisdom, one fills the inexhaustible ocean.
It is like those two great rivers, which are the color of purple-gold, bright and radiant, and whose sands are also the color of purple-gold.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Through the eloquence of dispatching [all things], it issues forth from the mouth; all sentient beings yearn for his body of wisdom, bringing joy to the entire world;
and with adamantine wisdom, he illuminates all that exists.
Universally delivering all beings, he constantly aspires to guide them through causes and conditions so that they may return to the ocean of wisdom;
furthermore, he is like the great river Bakṣu, which flows from the mouth of a bull, blue with the color of lapis lazuli, its brilliant current possessing a pure hue.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
He flows forth with inexhaustible, radiant eloquence;
through unimpeded dharmas, he possesses hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of majestic power.
Raining down from mindfulness, it flows into the River of Dharma and turns to fill the ocean of universal wisdom, culminating in the ocean of the Dharma-treasuries of all Buddhas;
like the confluence of those rivers, it swirls and circles in the four directions before returning to fill the great ocean.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
He turns his bodily conduct in accordance [with the Way], he turns his mental conduct in accordance [with the Way]; the turning of body, speech, and mind is fully perfected.
It is just like the currents of the four rivers flowing back to the sea.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
By means of the four adornments, they return to the ocean of universal wisdom.
What are these four?
First, adorning oneself by beholding all Buddhas;
second, beholding the Buddha’s discerning wisdom;
third, adorning oneself with the radiant light of the Buddhas' Dharma.
Fourth, to grasp all dhāraṇīs without doubt or confusion.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.
First, they take the various pāramitās as their adornment.
Second, they take the various bodhisattvas as the adornment of their conduct.
Third, they take the practice of great compassion as their adornment.
Fourth, he adorns all sentient beings by fulfilling them with the practice of the Wheel of Dharma.
These are the four.
"Just as that great river swirls seven times, it is adorned with four kinds of flowers—blue, red, yellow, and white."
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
With the mind of the Mahāyāna, he preaches the Dharma among those who have not yet been delivered in that interval, thereby causing them to arise [in awakening].
He distributes hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of various meditative absorptions and samādhis.

Universally beholding the virtues of the Buddhas throughout the three periods of time and across all Buddha-fields, their pure conduct is free from defilement; like that which is unarisen and tranquil, they are surrounded by trees of various jewels.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Surrounded by the adornments of all buddha-fields, he attains perfect enlightenment and manifests joy.
Just as that pool of water is stable, without movement or agitation, yet remains pure, clear, and transparent.
That bodhisattva is also like this!
That bodhisattva governs the mind with the Way and its virtue; it is tranquil, pure, clear, and transparent, fully endowed with the roots of countless virtues.
Just as that Lake Anavatapta has its shores made of various jewels, shining through from both within and without, pure and free from defilement;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva!

That Bodhisattva’s mind, by means of the ten jewel-like wisdoms, reaches up to hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of practices, attaining the supreme wisdom of vows and universally acquiring them, clearly understanding the root of all pure virtues.
Just as that [ocean] is without回流 (āvaartana), transparent both within and without, with a bottom of purple-gold sand adorned with various jewels,
so too is the Bodhisattva!

They attain penetrating wisdom through mental non-conceptuality, clarifying the realm of bodhisattvas; they adorn themselves with the virtues of all bodhisattvas, remaining unimpeded regarding all phenomena; they recognize that the practices of all buddhas have no fixed location, and they know the times and seasons of all practices with perfect clarity.
Just as those various dragons dwell there,
so too is the Bodhisattva!
He guides all worlds of terror, illuminating them completely, and universally protects all beings throughout the extreme reaches of the world.
"Just as that flowing water issues from four springs and flows onward, returning to the virtues of all Buddhas, gradually crossing over by boat and ferry until it reaches the ocean;
so too is the Bodhisattva!

By means of the four great rivers of wisdom, they universally moisten and nourish the realms of the devas, Brahmās, and Māras, as well as all śramaṇas and brahmins throughout the world, and all human beings at the height of existence; gradually ferrying them back to the unsurpassed ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom, they adorn themselves with the four kinds of power.
What are the four?
First is the wisdom of original vows, which universally rescues all beings in the extreme worlds.
Second is the wisdom directed toward non-interruption, which transforms and delivers all beings in the extreme worlds.
Third, to be fully endowed with the wisdom of the various pāramitās, causing one to rely upon the conduct of a bodhisattva and accord with purity.

Fourth, to clearly maintain the foundation of all sentient beings and clearly penetrate all thoughts, causing them to return to the unceasing stream and attain the ocean-like wisdom of the three periods of time.
These are the four.
To eliminate and cease dwelling [in worldly attachments] refers to the bodhisattva’s practice of meditative concentration and wisdom.
By means of countless samādhis, one adorns oneself with the ornaments of various jewels and beholds the Buddhas.
With the wisdom of non-viewing, they flow back to the ocean of all Buddhas;

with the practice of the wisdom of great compassion, their conduct likewise possesses great loving-kindness, guiding all beings in accordance with the truth without turning back, reaching the ultimate limit of arousal;
with immeasurable wisdom of skillful means, they return to the ocean of the ten powers.
"Just as those four rivers emerge from the Anavatapta Lake and flow toward the boundless great ocean, so it is with the Bodhisattva!

Practicing the supreme great vows and fulfilling all bodhisattva deeds, they attain all inexhaustible great wisdom; their manifold practices are likewise inexhaustible, and they constantly behold all Buddhas, taking this as their delight."
Just as those four great rivers flow without turning back toward the great ocean, never ceasing or being interrupted,
so it is with the Bodhisattva!
The vow of the Bodhisattva is free from all hindrance, attaining the radiant light of the fully perfected practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
They attain entry into the practice of universal wisdom and the path of awakening to all phenomena; through non-conceptualization and non-attachment, they cultivate the conduct of the Tathāgata.
Just as those four great rivers flow toward the ocean for kalpas without weariness or cessation, so do they proceed.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!

Cultivating entry into the practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, they cultivate the bodhisattva conduct for incalculable eons without weariness or fatigue, thereby achieving the return to the ocean of all Tathāgatas and the return to the practice of non-conceptualization.
It is like that great river which has no turning back, where the various jewels provide illumination,
the purple golden sand provides radiance,
and the silver sand provides brilliant shimmer.
The golden sands serve as radiant brilliance;

the lapis lazuli sands serve as a brilliant, shimmering glow. When the sunlight shines upon them, they completely eclipse the radiance of the sun. When their own brilliance reaches its peak, it penetrates beyond the sun, such that all created dwellings are free from any disturbance or affliction.
The radiance of that [Buddha] is beyond comparison; it is formed by the gathering of all manner of jewels.
It is the same with that Bodhisattva!

Having attained mastery over the Dharma-body and established himself in meditative concentration, from every single pore of his body, he universally emits the light of all Buddhas in infinite measure, whereby he perceives all lands and clearly enters the assemblies of beings.
Upon hearing the Dharma, they are able to receive and uphold it entirely; they clearly understand the countless bodily activities of the Tathāgata and penetrate the various Buddha-lands.

Seeing the assemblies of the Tathāgatas and hearing their preaching of the Dharma, through the attainment of non-attainment, they eliminate the long-standing conceptions of existence spanning billions of nayutas of kalpas.
Furthermore, there is no deficiency in his mindfulness; even regarding the hairs on his body, their number never decreases.
Nor does he dwell in discrimination concerning the various assemblies of Tathāgatas in all lands or the diverse realms of sentient beings.
Why is this? Because they have entered the Dharma-realm and because they employ the subtle understanding of non-self.
Furthermore, they do not enter into disparagement; they practice countless concentrations and cultivate countless practices.
Manifesting universally before all Buddhas, established by countless Buddhas, and moved by countless Buddhas, it is the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, the universal refuge from afar.
By means of the pure conduct of a bodhisattva and the ten powers of a Tathāgata, they are without obstruction.
They cultivate the practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, establishing it to full completion, and they thoroughly understand all manifestations without limit or hindrance.
So it is with the Bodhisattva!

Through a single moment of mind, they enter meditative absorption and awaken; they manifest themselves as exceedingly vast, yet they do not fall into the conduct they have entered and do not cling to any conditioned activities. Because they are free from the extremes of existence and non-existence, for the sake of all beings, they merely manifest the arising of Buddha-lands!

Within the *dharmadhātu*, they do not perceive the existence of lands or locations; they do not abide in limitations, nor do they abide between the two extremes. They cultivate and enter the wisdom of universal knowledge (*samantabhadra-jñāna*), delighting in and aspiring to the abiding in that wisdom, remaining free from self-aggrandizement, and understanding how to enter among the various classes of sentient beings.
They purify all lands, fully accomplishing the practices for all such lands, and thoroughly comprehend all manner of conceptualizations.
Not only does he transcend the places where various thoughts arise, but he also completely surpasses all manner of forms and appearances; having fully understood them, he remains undefiled.
Through the perfection of the Bodhisattva’s skillful wisdom, he reaches ultimate purity, becoming entirely free from conceptualization and universally establishing the stages of all practices.
"Just as reaching empty space, because one is detached from all realms of existence (*gati*), there is forever no further movement toward any realms of existence;
so too is the bodhisattva’s practice regarding buddha-fields!"
Thoroughly comprehending all lands, they practice to deliver sentient beings while forever abandoning all notions of "sentient beings.

They understand all dharma-realms and thereby eliminate all notions of "dharmas. They behold all Buddhas without weariness, aspiring to gaze upon them with reverence; they master all meditative concentrations and discern expedient practices, realizing that all dharmas are fundamentally pure and free from attachment.

Possessing the wisdom of inexhaustible dharma-verses and immeasurable eloquence, they clearly understand the absence of phrases and letters; they attain the practice of all sounds and realize the purity of sound, reaching the limit of the non-attainable Dharma while manifesting in various forms.

That which accords with and guides the objective realm is that all dharmas are fundamentally pure; yet, through ultimate great compassion, one takes pity upon and delivers the entire realm of sentient beings.
Without cause and without basis for cause, all realms are fundamentally pure; one thoroughly understands the dharma-realm in which one dwells as being without arising;
one thoroughly understands the various realms of existence as being without abiding, such that the three spheres are pure.

They thoroughly comprehend the conduct of the Tathāgata; they are free from conceptualization regarding diverse phenomena; they employ various skillful means and eloquent expositions to proclaim the Dharma with purity, thereby attaining the practice of the Dharma.
O son of noble family!
O bodhisattva mahāsattva!
You have attained adornment within the dharma-realm and are thus most venerable and great.
12. Chapter on the Great Skillful Wisdom of the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin:
"What, noble son, is the practice of the great skillful wisdom of the tenth supreme virtue of the great concentration of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas?"
"Noble son! Bodhisattvas possess a great samādhi called the 'Inexhaustible Field.
Those who enter into meditative absorption through this samādhi abide in the inexhaustibility of the activities of body, speech, and mind."
Abiding equally in all Buddha-fields is inexhaustible;
bringing sentient beings to liberation through their conduct is also inexhaustible;
and dwelling in the wisdom that guides sentient beings is likewise inexhaustible.
They emit rays of light that are inexhaustible;
they emit nets of radiance that are inexhaustible;
they manifest various emanations that are inexhaustible.
They attain the turning of the wheel of Dharma and yet it is inexhaustible;
their bodies can manifest as bodhisattvas or buddhas in all lands and yet they are inexhaustible. Their bodies fully realize the power of all buddhas;

their bodies aspire to the wisdom of all buddhas. They manifest the conduct of a buddha’s arising throughout all realms, moving from buddha to buddha, with a voice that penetrates everywhere, practicing the sanctity of a buddha and surpassing the deeds of a buddha.
His body transcends the measure of all Buddhas; he cultivates and perfects the Buddha-work, and his Buddha-conduct is sovereign. This is the samādhi of the ten supreme virtues.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, he contemplates universal wisdom (*sarvajñā*), clarifies universal wisdom, understands universal wisdom, attains mastery of universal wisdom, discriminates universal wisdom, manifests universal wisdom, distinguishes universal wisdom, beholds universal wisdom, enters into universal wisdom, and extensively reveals universal wisdom.
These are the ten.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not aspire for the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, nor for the mind of a great bodhisattva, nor for the conduct of a great bodhisattva, nor for what is manifested in practice, nor for the great world-systems entered and manifested, nor for their destinations and foundations, nor for the moistening grace of those great bodhisattvas; yet, even so, the great bodhisattva remains uninterrupted.
These are the ten. Furthermore, there are ten practices:

first, non-retrogression; second, lack of nourishment; third, lack of returning; fourth, lack of weariness; fifth, not thinking "I am" nor even the thought of non-thought; sixth, neither abandoning nor relinquishing; seventh, lack of agitation; eighth, lack of severance; ninth, not taking sound to be a bodhisattva.
These are the ten.
Why is this so? Because that bodhisattva has brought forth great vows regarding all dharmas and has fully perfected all practices.

The Great Way they have aroused consists entirely of the well-cultivated study of the ocean of the Buddha-dharma, the supreme and equal vows, and the bodhisattva practices; it clearly demonstrates the illumination of skillful means, wisdom, and expedient methods.
They are established by having well studied the illusory transformations of a bodhisattva and being thoroughly proficient in all sounds;
they are established by skillfully establishing [the understanding of] the past, future, present, and all worlds of the Buddhas;
and they are established by attaining the practice of great compassion.
By means of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one accomplishes the karma of the Buddha-dharma and brings forth the Buddha-dharma without obstruction.
This is the tenth. Why is this so?

It is, for example, like a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel; whatever they intend will be established without exception, and its radiance appears exactly according to their mental image, such that the mani-jewel remains no different from its original state.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Having attained the establishment of the wish-fulfilling jewel, they never tire of wisdom.
Repeatedly clarifying the wisdom of universal knowledge, they remain untiring in the conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
Just as a mani jewel manifests all its various colors and forms without destroying the essential nature of the jewel,
so it is with the Bodhisattva!
They bring about the manifestation of the image of universal wisdom, yet they do not destroy the essence of their original practice.
Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva’s aspiration is for the sake of all beings;
desiring to deliver all beings, he makes vows and cultivates the practices of all Buddhas without turning back.
Desiring to purify all Buddhas, they are without weariness because they undertake all things; thus, they never retreat in their tirelessness.
Regarding all infinite dharmas, they have no notion of a self, no rejection, and no weariness, universally manifesting all manner of spiritual transformations.
Having attained purity regarding sentient beings, they never grow weary, benefiting the entire world without ever retreating in their tirelessness.
Universally illuminating the world, they do not weary or retreat; entering the midst of the illusions of countless dharmas, they do not turn back, for their minds never regress.
This is called the ten.
"For example, just as red and yellow [colors] abide nowhere in empty space, that which is sustained by them does not give rise to weariness or fatigue, nor is it weakened;
it does not attain any mental state, has no location, is without bondage, has nothing seen, does not dwell within, nor does it dwell without."
Contemplating that there is no place within, one does not destroy original purity. Why is this?
Because the dharma of empty space is fundamentally pure.
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
Because they practice vast and boundless vows, they do not give rise to weariness or fatigue, for they act to bring forth the universal salvation of all sentient beings.
For example, regarding one who has entered parinirvāṇa: for what kind of person would there be such a parinirvāṇa?
Within the three periods of time, they are without limit; they experience neither fatigue, nor fear, nor do they ever turn back.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are non-dual.
As for those who have returned to nirvana, why would they undergo such toil?
The Bodhisattva is also like this!
He appears in the world solely for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the universe;
